articles.title_orig: California man smuggled $300 million in Nvidia chips to China, prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: California man smuggled $300 million in Nvidia chips to China, prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
A California man is facing federal charges for helping smuggle over $300 million worth of Nvidia semiconductor chips into China, prosecutors said this week.
Yiu Kong Lui, 38, of San Gabriel, Cali., was arrested on Thursday and is set to be arraigned in federal court and charged with violating export controls, smuggling, and money laundering, court records show.
It is illegal to export advanced semiconductor chips into China without a license, as the US competes with the East Asian giant in the AI race.
President Donald Trump drew criticism last year for allowing Nvidia to sell its chips to China , a departure from the previous US policy under President Joe Biden, which effectively blocked all exports of advanced chips to China.
Nvidia's chips are especially sought after for use in AI data centers because they can perform multiple calculations simultaneously, and because the company's software stack is widely compatible.
In a press release, US officials said Liu put US national security at risk by smuggling the chips.
"Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for America's businesses and economic security," said Roman Rozhavsky, an assistant director of the FBI's counterintelligence and espionage division.
It was not immediately clear on Friday whether Liu was being represented by an attorney. According to court records, Lui has not yet pleaded guilty or not guilty to the charges.
In a 22-page indictment, prosecutors said Liu worked with several co-conspirators who operated shell companies to first get the chips to either Malaysia or Singapore, and then into China.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Prosecutors said a company owned by Liu served as a go-between for foreign shipping companies and US chip manufacturers, and that Liu lied to US companies, claiming the chips wouldn't end up in China.
The operation began in 2023 and continued until August, according to the indictment. Liu's company was paid over $180 million by Malaysian shipping companies to broker the chip deals, prosecutors said.
If convicted of all charges, Liu could serve a combined 50 years in prison.
Nvidia did not immediately return a request for comment on Friday.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Europe agrees to release diesel stocks, Trump says
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Europe agrees to release diesel stocks, Trump says
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump said European leaders have agreed to release a "massive amount" of their diesel oil stockpiles to alleviate high prices, following an emergency meeting of the Group of Seven leaders.
A G7 video conference convened Friday morning to discuss fuel supply and prices, after a call overnight between French President Emmanuel Macron and Mr. Trump. After that meeting, Mr. Trump said Europe would release diesel oil from its stockpiles, beginning "immediately."
"Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The process will begin immediately. Thank you for your attention to this matter!"
A joint statement from G7 leaders released by the Élysée Palace in Paris confirmed a "coordinated release" of 100 million barrels that is to begin immediately and will take place over a four-month period. This will include a "front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners," the statement said.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the U.S., including the European Union as a non-enumerated member.
A White House official said Mr. Trump spoke with Macron last night and with the G7 leaders this morning to negotiate the release of European diesel stockpiles.
Mr. Trump has threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports, a move that would push global diesel prices even higher. In their statement, the G7 leaders discouraged any such bans, but did not mention Mr. Trump.
"We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions," the statement said.
In the U.S., soaring diesel prices are rippling through the economy, putting a financial squeeze on schools, farmers and small businesses as their fuel costs spike. Farmers, who rely on diesel to run agricultural machinery, also face much higher costs, while enterprises ranging from construction firms to food banks have been reporting sharply increased expenses to fuel their vehicles and delivery trucks.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
Margaret  Brennan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 2031 Women’s World Cup bid update on agenda for FIFA Council meeting
articles.title_zh: 2031 Women’s World Cup bid update on agenda for FIFA Council meeting
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA Council will hear an update on the bid process for the 2031 Women’s World Cup, which is tentatively slated to be held in the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, at its Oct. 14 meeting. It will be the first such update since FIFA delayed the vote on awarding the event to the four nations from its Congress this past April to an Extraordinary Congress on Nov. 23.
The joint bid from the four Concacaf nations , submitted last November, is the only one for the 2031 Women’s World Cup. It included 35 prospective host cities: 27 in the U.S., six in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica.
Because of the one-sided nature of the host city agreements for the 2026 men’s World Cup, however, the prospective U.S. host cities refused to agree to specific hosting terms before the 2031 bid was submitted. They are seeking an opportunity to negotiate more favorable terms that would reduce their financial and operational burdens while providing greater revenue opportunities.
It is unknown whether any meaningful discussions have taken place since the conclusion of the men’s World Cup regarding new terms for the 2031 Women’s World Cup. U.S. Soccer is expected to play a role in facilitating those discussions after largely being sidelined in the delivery of the men’s World Cup.
The Women’s World Cup bidding update will also touch on the 2035 Women’s World Cup, for which the U.K. is the lone bidder. Other notable agenda items for the Oct. 14 meeting include a review of President Gianni Infantino’s controversial FIFA Forward Enterprise investment proposal, which was scrapped following massive backlash , as well as reviews of FIFA’s reserves and the financing of its member associations. The agenda also mentions a discussion of the FIFA Peace Prize, which was awarded for the first time in 2025 to President Trump .
The FIFA Council has 37 members, including representatives elected through each of the six regional confederations. U.S. Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone sits on the council as Concacaf’s North American representative.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Higher, Yields Fall as Hiring Softens — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Higher, Yields Fall as Hiring Softens — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks rose Friday, though were off their highs, following a surprisingly weak jobs report that raised hopes the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady in October.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 178 points, or 0.3%. The S&P 500 gained 0.7%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.2%, hitting an all-time high earlier in the day before retreating slightly from those levels.
Treasury yields fell Friday initially following the employment report, though they rebounded, pushing U.S. equities off their highs for the session.
Tech stocks rallied as risk-taking resumed on Wall Street, with shares of Nvidia hitting an all-time high for the first time since May. CrowdStrike , Palo Alto Networks and AMD also all rose to all-time highs. Meanwhile, shares of Intel and AMD also rose 2% and 3%, respectively.
September's nonfarm payrolls report showed the U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs last month, with unemployment rising to 4.2%. The Dow Jones consensus called for jobs growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
"This is the exact kind of number the market wanted from a labor standpoint," said Phil Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic. "Not too hot, not too cold ... not overly great, and not weakening."
That number made traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 78% likelihood the central bank will stand pat at this month's meeting, up from a roughly 76% chance just the prior day, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
Saira Malik, chief investment officer at Nuveen, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the report may give the market support before earnings season kicks off, which she thinks will be "very strong."
"So, I think this could be the start of the Santa Claus rally that we've all been hoping for," she said.
Oil prices pulled back , supporting equities, following a report that European nation states are considering a release of strategic fuel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
Investors are coming off a modestly higher session Thursday, to start off the month of October. However, the Dow and the S&P 500 were headed for weekly losses amid a global bond rout, while the Nasdaq was the only major average on pace to end the week with gains.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed to this report
Tesla deliveries in the third quarter beat Wall Street's expectations on Friday, coming at 486,532 versus 461,100 expected.
Deliveries eased from 497,099 in the year-ago period but climbed up from the second quarter's 480,126 delivered vehicles.
Shares were up in morning trading on Friday.
The Grayscale Zcash ETF (ZCSH) is up more than 60% in the past month, bringing its year-to-date gain to about 253%, thanks to renewed interest in privacy as speculative capital this year has rotated into AI.
Zcash (ZEC) itself – up more than 170% this year compared to bitcoin , which is stagnant on the year – was designed to keep users' financial transactions completely private. It launched in 2016, but the privacy narrative eventually faded as privacy coins became a compliance headache for regulators and exchanges.
Crypto's mainstream investment case has become increasingly institutionalized and transparent, while AI has made large-scale financial surveillance and transaction analysis more powerful. The combination of the two has allowed the privacy narrative to gain traction and lead to the launch of the Grayscale Zcash ETF in August.
By comparison, the popular iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) is down about 1% this year and the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index ETF (BITW) , which tracks the 10 largest cryptocurrencies, is down 5%. Meanwhile, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has gained 12% and the Invesco QQQ is up nearly 22%.
Nvidia popped on Friday, briefly hitting an all-time intraday high.
Shares of the semiconductor firm rose more than 3% to as much as $237.88 on the day. At its peak, the stock traded at its highest intraday level ever.
Nvidia's shares began trading on the public market in January 1999.
Revisions in the September jobs report for July and August are making those months look weaker for job creation.
July was marked down by 31,000 to mark a net job loss of 10,000 on the month, the Labor Department reported Friday. August was marked down by 29,000 for a new total of 133,000 compared to the initial robust report of 162,000.
"Revisions made both July and August look weaker, too. Over the past 3 months, we've an average of a mere +17k per month," economist Justin Wolfers wrote on social media .
Stocks opened higher Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 322 points, or 0.6%. The S&P 500 gained 0.8%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.1%.
The latest fed funds futures trading showed an 86% likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady when it convenes for its Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. That's up from a roughly 76% chance just one day prior.
The U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate increased to 4.2 percent in September as job creation slowed substantially during the month, the Labor Department reported Friday.
Economists were expecting 84,000 new payrolls and the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
Here are some of the names moving premarket:
Click here to see more stocks making moves.
Shares for Seagate Technology and Western Digital slipped over 10% and 8% respectively after Toshiba announced plans to double its production capacity for hard disk drives used in data centers, according to a Nikkei report.
The Japanese company plans to invest $380 million to expand facilities in the Philippines, signaling Toshiba's first major hard disk drives investment in about five years, Nikkei reported.
Toshiba, along with Seagate Technology and Western Digital, are the top competitors in the hard disk drives market.
Morgan Stanley put Nvidia back atop its list of semiconductor stocks on Friday, touting the company's range of customers and the importance of graphics processing units (GPUs) to agentic artificial intelligence.
"While 90% of investor conversations are around the biggest hyperscalers and frontier model companies, half of the business - probably the faster growing half - is a broader range of AI model companies, Neoclouds, sovereign entities, ODMs and OEMs, and enterprise customers," Joseph Moore at Morgan Stanley wrote in a Friday note to clients.
Moore has an overweight rating on the stock with price target of $300 and an "industry view" listed as "attractive."
With its numerous backstopping and vendor agreements during the AI boom, Nvidia has faced criticism for being involved in circular financing during the AI buildout, which interlinks Nvidia's investments with its eventual revenue streams.
Oil prices fell more than 2% on Friday morning, extending losses from earlier in the session, following reports of a potential European move to release diesel and crude stocks to ease a global supply shortage
International benchmark Brent crude futures with December expiry traded 2.5% lower at $99.78 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry fell nearly 3.8% to $89.40.
It comes shortly after Reuters reported that European Union member states were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
Moderna will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the tech-heavy blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index after the biotech's shares have risen nearly sixfold over the past year.
The change will take effect before the market opens on Oct. 9, the stock exchange said in a statement late Thursday.
Shares of Moderna rose 2.4% in premarket trading, adding to a 563% gain over the past 12 months.
The company, which became a household name after it developed one of the first vaccines for Covid-19, surprised the Street last month when an experimental personalized cancer vaccine co-developed with Merck showed positive initial results in its first-ever late-stage trial.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Haitians remain in the grip of lethal gang violence as it continues to “adapt and expand”, the UN’s top rights official, Volker Türk, said on Friday.
In an update to the Human Rights Council , the High Commissioner welcomed the first Gang Suppression Force operations, mandated by the UN Security Council .
These will help boost security in Haiti “but the Force remains far below the strength needed”, Mr. Türk insisted, in support of its “full, accelerated deployment” with human rights safeguards embedded.
At least 5,700 people have been confirmed killed or injured by gangs – or during operations against them – since 1 January, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR .
Gang members have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped at least 1,000 women and girls. The real figures are likely much higher, Mr. Türk said.
In his update, the High Commissioner for Human Rights also warned that “extortion, looting and destruction of property” are crippling economic activity in Haiti.
The “constant danger” prevents people from reaching schools, hospitals, and essential services, Mr. Türk stressed.
Three hijacked ships have been freed after months in captivity, but five seafarers died during the rescue of one of them, the head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has said.
IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez offered his condolences after the operation to free the HONOUR 25 in Somali waters on 29 September, in which several other crew members were seriously injured.
Mr. Dominguez said seafarers “should not have to lose their lives for the service they provide for the world”, and called for renewed resolve, targeted cooperation and the resources needed to stop piracy in the region.
The HONOUR 25 was one of three vessels released this week, along with the SEAMULL (also known as SIBU 1) and the MT EUREKA, all seized between April and August by pirates and armed robbers.
In total, 44 seafarers were freed and their governments are working to arrange their repatriation. Mr. Dominguez thanked Somalia's Government for its efforts, but noted that 22 seafarers remain captive aboard the ASANA.
He urged Governments to bring new initiatives, such as the proposed Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, to the IMO, and stressed the importance of the EUNAVFOR Aspides and Atalanta operations for maritime security in the region.
An additional 11.7 million women and girls in 28 countries could face food insecurity by the end of the year due to the escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
These crises are driving up food prices and putting a strain on livelihoods and household resources, UN Women said in new analysis published on Friday.
Presenting the findings to journalists in Geneva, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said the estimates are a potential scenario, not a forecast, and that the number is in addition to the 208 million women and girls who were already estimated to be food insecure or malnourished in these countries.
“Experience from past conflicts shows that when food is scarce, women often reduce the amount they eat or skip meals so that children and other family members can eat,” she said.
The greatest numbers of women and girls at risk are in populous countries, while South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen and Palestine face the highest concentration of overlapping vulnerabilities.
UN Women recommends linking food and cash assistance to nutrition, protection, employment and agricultural services. Women should also have access to land, credit and productive resources.
The agency also highlighted the need for better collection of data that shows where food insecurity is worsening and who is eating less, losing income and carrying the heaviest burden of unpaid care work.

articles.title_orig: Why Lilly and Novo are betting on amylin to power a new wave of obesity drugs after GLP-1s
articles.title_zh: Why Lilly and Novo are betting on amylin to power a new wave of obesity drugs after GLP-1s
articles.content_orig:
The next generation of blockbuster obesity drugs isn't trying to replace GLP-1 medicines.
Instead, drugmakers are developing treatments that can complement existing drugs and push weight loss further, or offer new options for potentially millions of people who may not get enough benefit from GLP-1s.
That's the early potential of a new slate of injections, pills, and combination regimens targeting the amylin pathway, which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness. Amylin gives Eli Lilly and Novo another biological lever to pull in treating obesity and Type 2 diabetes, either as an independent treatment or layered on top of existing drugs.
Lilly offered a promising glimpse of that strategy this week.
The company's experimental amylin-targeting drug, eloralintide, helped produce substantially more weight loss when combined with tirzepatide – the active ingredient in its blockbuster Zepbound and Mounjaro shots – in a Phase 2 trial on patients with obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
At 48 weeks, people receiving the highest-dose combination lost an average of 23.3% of their body weight, compared with 14.8% among those only taking a high dose of tirzepatide. Those figures are based on efficacy analysis that assumes patients remained on treatment in the trial.
"These are encouraging results," said Benjamin Bikman, a professor at Brigham Young University and leading expert on metabolic health and insulin resistance.  "Adults with type 2 diabetes typically lose less weight on these therapies than those without diabetes."
Lilly is developing eloralintide both as a standalone treatment and as part of that combo therapy. The two components make up what some analysts view as a major future franchise for the company.
Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger forecasts $23.2 billion in annual sales for Lilly's eloralintide products by the end of 2035. He said he expects the standalone drug to launch first in 2029, followed by the combo in 2030.
"There are millions of individuals, potentially over 10 million people, who have tried GLP-1s and failed due to efficacy reasons, tolerability issues, or genetic issues where they simply do not respond to one," Risinger told CNBC. "We think this novel mechanism, this amylin analog … will offer a major new treatment alternative for patients, both as a monotherapy and as a combination therapy. "
Risinger said he sees greater potential for standalone eloralintide given the "huge independent patient pool" that hasn't seen success on existing GLP-1s. Lilly still sees a clear opportunity for pairing the medications.
"Patients may not get what they need from a drug like tirzepatide," Ken Custer, president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in an interview. "They may not get what they need from a drug like a eloralintide on its own."
Bikman also said he sees the combo as an opportunity for patients who started on tirzepatide alone but saw their weight loss plateau.
But Lilly still has a lot to prove. The data comes from a relatively small Phase 2 study that the company will need to confirm in Phase 3 trials, which will begin later this year.
Lilly also aims to improve how well patients tolerate the combo regimen in later studies. More patients taking both drugs — 10.8% to 27%, depending on the dose — discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared with the 2.9% of people on tirzepatide alone in the trial.
"A therapy is only effective if patients can remain on it, so tolerability in Phase 3 will be as important as efficacy," Bikman said.
Dr. Caroline Apovian, co-director of the Center for Weight Management and Wellness at Brigham and Women's Hospital, added that "27% is not a good number."
Still, the results add to a growing body of evidence that amylin could become an important tool against obesity and diabetes.
Lilly isn't alone in betting that amylin can become a building block for the next generation of obesity drugs. Novo has spent years pursuing a similar strategy.
Novo's experimental amylin-based drug, cagrilintide, has shown meaningful weight loss as a standalone treatment in a late-stage trial. Combining it with semaglutide – together dubbed CagriSema – has produced even greater weight loss in clinical studies. CagriSema is expected to launch early next year, followed by standalone cagrilintide and a higher-dose version of CagriSema in 2028.
Novo is also developing another treatment called amycretin, or zenagamtide, which is a single molecule that would target both GLP-1 and amylin to treat obesity and Type 2 diabetes. The Danish drugmaker is testing it as a once-weekly injection and a daily oral tablet, and the drug showed promising Phase 2 results earlier this year.
The first – and so far only – amylin therapy was approved in the U.S. more than two decades ago as an add-on mealtime injection for people with diabetes who use insulin. But adoption was limited in part because it required multiple injections a day.
New therapies in development are long-acting, meaning they are designed to mimic the hormone in a sustained way and can be taken once a week, Bikman said.
Amylin helps signal fullness, suppress appetite and slow the movement of food through the stomach, similar to what GLP-1 does. But amylin achieves that by acting on an entirely different biological pathway.
"It's the same outcome, but a different approach," Bikman told CNBC.
The idea is that targeting multiple pathways could produce more weight loss or other metabolic benefits than any single pathway can achieve on its own, and without relying entirely on higher doses of a single drug.
New data from Novo this week suggests that the benefits could go beyond physical changes.
CagriSema reduced "food noise" — persistent thoughts about food — and showed improvements to organ and bone health in a yearlong functional magnetic resonance imaging study, which is a noninvasive method to measure brain activity during specific tasks. Novo said CagriSema changed how the brain reacted to tempting, high-calorie foods in areas linked to cravings, pleasure and self-control in people with obesity or who were overweight.
"The signal in the brain changes in a way that actually is associated with improved quality of life," Martin Holst Lange, Novo's chief scientific officer, said in an interview.
Developing treatments that target several hormone pathways rather than one is part of a broader shift in the obesity drug race, even beyond amylin.
Tirzepatide already pairs GLP-1 with GIP, while Lilly's experimental drug retatrutide also adds glucagon to the mix. Retatrutide has produced some of the largest weight loss results reported in obesity drug trials to date, and Bikman said published data on the drug demonstrate substantial reductions in liver fat, triglycerides and fasting insulin.
It's too early to definitively say whether combination amylin drugs could be superior to tirzepatide or other next-generation treatments. They'll have to clear more clinical trials and regulatory reviews first.
But all the medicines in development are working toward a broader goal shared by several drugmakers: giving patients a variety of obesity and diabetes treatment options to meet their individualized needs.

articles.title_orig: Funny old world: the week's offbeat news
articles.title_zh: Funny old world: the week's offbeat news
articles.content_orig:
From "seal silly season" to why Nigerians are obsessed with breaking records... Your weekly roundup of offbeat stories from around the world:
- 'Nigerians don't come last' -
Another triumph for Nigeria's growing army of record breakers, after the man who climbed 150 steps on a ladder balancing a football on his head, and the guy who spun a plate on his finger for two whole hours.
Dancer Benjamin Daniel Gabriel boogied for more than a week to shimmy his way to Guinness World Records glory.
He has become the latest national hero in a country that has become obsessed with over-the-top endurance stunts.
Chef Hilda Baci started the craze in 2023 with the longest cooking marathon, making jollof rice and other local delicacies for 93 hours and 11 minutes.
"Nigerians don't come last in anything," Tunde Onakoya, who holds the record for the longest chess marathon, told AFP as Gabriel danced in the background.
"We like to test ourselves against the world -- we are capable of all forms of greatness."
- Rice work gives Dutch courage -
From the land that brought us watery winter tomatoes, comes chewy rice. Those ingenious Dutch have found a way of using their sinking polders to grow sushi rice and possibly make a new form of Dutch courage -- sake.
A pilot paddy between The Hague and Amsterdam has yielded a promising harvest and local restaurants want to serve the rice produced. "It tasted delicious," said Guusje van der Vossen of regenerative nature group Wij Land. "It was a bit chewy, but also great."
Why did the seal cross the road? To get to the train, of course.
New Zealand police came to the rescue of a wandering seal who had crossed a busy road in the capital Wellington and seemed to be making its way to its main railway station.
"The pup appeared grateful for the assistance," said the police, who returned it to the sea, though no one asked the seal.
Its adventures are the latest in a long line of bizarre encounters with the marine mammals during New Zealand's "seal silly season".
Last year another pup waddled up from the sea and into a bar in Richmond on the other side of the Cook Strait. It left without buying a drink, but may have been put off with the owner shouting "Hide the salmon!" when he saw him.
- Masseur gets rubbed up -
A Slovakian masseur will take on the best cyclists on the planet on Sunday after his country's top riders were forced to pull out of the World Championships.
Vladimir Kovacik, 28, has not raced in a decade since he finished in 32nd place in a time trial back home.
But when the country's top three riders were forced to drop out of the race in Montreal -- because of injuries for two of them and a contractual issue for one -- the team turned to its surprised masseur to keep the Central European country's flag flying.
Slovakia's cycling federation admitted it was "not ideal" but Kovacik putting himself through the wringer would help keep their place among cycling's elite, they said.

articles.title_orig: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.title_zh: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.content_orig:
Gino has proudly served the Tonawanda community from 351 Fries Road since opening his doors in 1983.
Now in his fourth decade of making pizza at his eponymous restaurant in Tonawanda, Gino Pinzone is a part of the old guard who made Buffalo pizza a thing. At seventy years old, he still gets behind the counter of Gino’s Pizza Place at 9 a.m. to make dough, prep sauce, and mentor a new generation of employees.
You’ve been a fixture in the local food scene for decades. Where did that passion for cooking begin?
Everything started back in Sicily. My mother had eleven children, so she worked at home day and night, night and day, constantly cooking for fourteen people. I’m number eight, so I did a lot of helping, making everything you could possibly make at home. I still do it for myself today. I learned everything from her.
Did she teach you to bake?
In those days, we really could not afford meat. Bread was everything. Chinese people use rice. Mexicans use tortilla shells. We were heavy on bread. When it came out of the oven, it was a treat just to put extra virgin olive oil and black pepper on it. That was it.
How did you end up owning a pizzeria?
I went to Buffalo State for Industrial Arts; I was going to be a teacher. But in 1978, my older brother opened a pizzeria and asked me and my brother Frank to work for him. I liked it a lot. I never finished my master's degree in teaching because I was doing okay making pizzas with my brother! I opened my first solo place in November 1983, and here I am today.
What do you love the most?
My employees. Some started as high school students from across the street. They start folding boxes and then, little by little, I teach them how to do a few things here and there. They might go away for college, but they always come back. It’s rewarding. Take care of the employees because the employees will always take care of you. And that’s what they do. I trust them, and they do a great job.
It sounds almost like a family atmosphere .
I get kids coming in who might be a little quiet or shy. Their parents ask if I can hire them, to get them out of their bedrooms and away from the video games. Next thing you know, they’re hopping around and working and loving it. I tell them, “You’re learning a skill.”
It’s not just about making pizzas but also learning how to get around a restaurant. You need to do dishes, you need to cut celery, you need to do this... Even if they graduate and get a degree, they can go anywhere in the world and work in a pizzeria because they know how a kitchen moves.
Many of the restaurant’s Instagram reels feature you. Do you enjoy being in the spotlight?
[Laughs] My son Phil does all that! He puts the camera in my face and says, “Dad, we’re introducing eggplant pizza today.” I always tell him, “Phil, I’m not doing a second take.” Whatever comes out of me, comes out. We did one video recently that had 20,000 viewers. People come in now just because they want to see me and talk to me.
Why have you never expanded to a second location?
I want to be totally responsible for everything that comes out of the place. I do all the prep work. I’m there from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. every day. On Fridays, I’m there until dinner is over. On Sundays, I’m there until the Bills game is over.  Nobody does it like the owner. It’s hard to train somebody to do things the way I do. Nowadays, people open five places and there’s no personal feeling.
And after forty years, most people would be taking it easy. What keeps you coming back every morning?
It’s not the money. It’s the DNA of a pizza guy in me. I see regulars who came in as kids now bringing their own grandkids in and putting them up on my counter. Why would I walk away? It makes it all worthwhile.

articles.title_orig: Gold & The Battalion Approved to Transition to World Class
articles.title_zh: Gold & The Battalion Approved to Transition to World Class
articles.content_orig:
REBROADCAST: Texas Marching Classic
Massive drum corps news just dropped.
DCI Open Class veterans Gold and The Battalion have both been approved to transition into the World Class beginning with the 2027 DCI Summer Tour.
All of the Bands Competing at the 2027 Texas Marching Classic 🤠   | BOA Weekend Watch Guide, Oct. 3 🗓️   | Troopers Announce DCI 2027 Show Title 👀   | Recent Marching Headlines You May Have Missed 🔥   | WATCH LIVE on October 17: Texas Marching Classic 🤠
After a successful vote by DCI's member organizations in addition to a multi-year examination of the organizations' finances and operations, both Gold and The Battalion are excited to endeavor on a new adventure in their new class.
A recent success story of the transition from Open Class to World Class is Spartans, which just completed its first full season as a DCI World Class member with their show, 'On the World Stage.'
Here's what the two ensembles had to say to DCI about the move:
“This is a culmination of everything we’ve been building over the last 12 years. For our staff and members, there’s definitely excitement, but I think it will mostly feel like a natural next step, because we’ve always seen ourselves as headed in this direction. We’ve been incredibly honored by the new fans we’ve met on the road as our tours have grown longer each year. We’re excited to grow that community as we take this step.” - Tyler Hess, director of The Battalion
“Moving into World Class is a big moment for Gold. It’s something we’ve been working toward for a long time, even if it wasn’t always the immediate goal in front of us. We’ve always worked hard to make drum corps accessible and to create a place where members can grow as performers and as people. That remains important to us regardless of what classification we compete in.” - Kevin Valentine, executive director of Gold
To read DCI's full press release, click here.
The Battalion had a breakout year, earning the silver medal at DCI Open Class World Championships (81.500) and 20th at DCI World Championship Semifinals (79.225).
Gold finished out the 2026 DCI season placing third at DCI Open Class World Championships (80.300) and 22nd at DCI World Championship Semifinals (77.975).
Interested in marching Gold or The Battalion in 2027? Click here for more information about Gold's audition process , and here for more information about The Battalion's audition process.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats slam ‘Trump’s failing economic agenda’ after weaker-than-expected jobs growth – US politics live
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats slam ‘Trump’s failing economic agenda’ after weaker-than-expected jobs growth – US politics live
articles.content_orig:
Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer criticize president after US added 29,000 new jobs in September, sharply less than the 84,000 economists had predicted
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Elizabeth Warren , the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, has blasted Donald Trump’s “failing economic agenda” following the latest jobs report – which many experts have described as “mediocre” and “weak”.
“Since January 2025, Trump’s economy has only added 33,000 jobs a month on average, far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024,” Warren said. “Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7% as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up.”
Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats are hammering home that many of the Trump administration’s policies have resulted in a cost of living crisis, and urging voters to eschew Republicans vying for seats in Congress at the ballot box.
Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.
As we bring you the news of the deal that European leaders have struck to releases millions of barrels of diesel reserves, a White House official tells the Guardian that Donald Trump spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday night , and with G7 leaders on Friday morning, to successfully negotiate the release of the stockpiles .
This detail comes after the administration publicly urged the leaders to tap into the reserves, and Trump has floated a possible diesel export ban, which Europe has warned would be economically crippling.
The White House has welcomed the latest jobs report – which shows fewer new jobs added than economists projected. Taylor Rogers, a spokesperson, highlighted the addition of “9,000 manufacturing jobs and 12,300 factory construction jobs over the month” as proof that Donald Trump’s “reindustrialization agenda is working” .
She noted that “wages are up over last year” – despite the fact they have not kept up with inflation.
Pete Hegseth , the US defense secretary, announced today that there will be a “one-day stand-down” this month, for service members to vote in the upcoming midterm elections. He added that many members of the military “face unnecessary, difficult ways of obtaining, completing, and returning absentee ballots while serving far from home” and said the directive would take place this year and every election year to come.
“We’re not telling you who to vote for, but we will give you every opportunity to do so,” Hegseth said in a straight-to-camera video. “Take that day to fill out your absentee ballot. Help your family members do the same, or go to the polling place yourself and exercise your right to vote.”
My colleagues are covering the move from G7 leaders to release up to 100m barrels of diesel reserves within four months, to mitigate the ongoing energy crisis as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Earlier, as I reported, Trump welcomed the news after urging European countries this week to tap into reserves while he weighed an export ban. However, the president offered few details about which countries had signed on to the deal.
On today’s episode of Politics Weekly America, Jonathan Freedland is digging into the Texas Senate race.
The Democratic Senate nominee, James Talarico , is surprising everyone, as polls have him leading his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton .
Jonathan speaks to James Henson , founder and executive director of the Texas Politics Project, about why a blue wave in the Lone Star state – which hasn’t seen a Democrat win a Senate seat in almost 40 years – would be seismic.
On Truth Social, Donald Trump has claimed that Europe has “just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil”. This comes after the administration urged European allies to release their diesel reserves as fuel prices continue to rise due to the ongoing Iran war and the president continues to weigh an export ban. The president added that “the process will begin immediately” .
In the US the average price for a gallon of diesel sits at $6.3, up from $3.7 a year ago – a 70% hike.
Trump said on Wednesday that he was still “thinking about” a ban on diesel exports to curb the soaring cost of energy domestically. However, he noted that an embargo “might raise the price of other things.” Europe has warned of a further economic tailspin in the event of a ban.
A reminder that major sectors of US agriculture, manufacturing and commercial fishing depend heavily on diesel.
Europe has also becoming increasingly reliant on US diesel exports after Ukrainian strikes destroyed Russian oil refineries and Moscow implemented its own export ban earlier this year to preserve its supply.
And as we bring you the latest on how the jobs report stands to impact voter sentiment ahead of the November midterms , my colleagues have done all the hard work in mapping out the battle for Congress and the key states, candidates and districts that will ultimately decide the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives , and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.
A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest market reactions to today’s job report, including allayed fears about future interest rate hikes in light of the weaker-than-expected numbers reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Since January 2025, Trump’s economy has only added 33,000 jobs a month on average, far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024,” Warren said. “Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7% as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up.”
Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats are hammering home that many of the Trump administration’s policies have resulted in a cost of living crisis, and urging voters to eschew Republicans vying for seats in Congress at the ballot box.
Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.
Of note, the wage growth according to the latest jobs report, sits at 3% – which is still lower than the current 3.4% inflation rate. The gap here is crucial as voters prepare to vote in the upcoming midterms, and affordability is consistently polled as the key election issue ahead of November.
New figures, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, shows that the number of new jobs added in the US was weaker than expected, while unemployment saw an uptick.
The US added 29,000 new jobs in September, significantly fewer than the roughly 90,000 economists forecasted. Unemployment increased slightly to 4.2% – up by 0.1 point compared to last month’s data.
The latest report shows a drop in the overall number of jobs in September, compared to August , where the revised numbers show that the US added 133,000 new jobs.
Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington after spending Thursday campaigning in Durant, Oklahoma. He’ll travel to Mobile, Alabama, at 12.30pm ET today for a campaign rally. It’s part of the president’s 32-day blitz to juice support for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections. He won Mobile county by almost 17 points in the 2024 presidential election.
Despite the president initially saying that he would focus his attention on competitive districts, in recent days he’s made speeches in Republican strongholds as his approval rating is still under water.

articles.title_orig: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.title_zh: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination” .
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates , where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

articles.title_orig: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive thanks to AI
articles.title_zh: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive thanks to AI
articles.content_orig:
The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When we talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project , but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that the Shield is still being actively manufactured and that the company sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As one of the key players in AI hyperscaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo , Microsoft , and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store , but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy .

articles.title_orig: Milwaukee Tool Joins Alliance for America's Skilled Trades
articles.title_zh: Milwaukee Tool Joins Alliance for America's Skilled Trades
articles.content_orig:
Milwaukee Tool announced it has joined the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, a national effort bringing together companies committed to strengthening the skilled trades workforce and expanding pathways into rewarding careers.
The company joins the Alliance with a longstanding commitment to the people and organizations building the skilled trades workforce across the United States.
For more than 100 years, the company has built its business around serving the professional trades. Since 2010 alone, Milwaukee Tool has invested in workforce development initiatives supporting skilled trades education, training and career pathways. Based on current and planned investment, that investment is expected to exceed $200 million by 2030.
“Milwaukee Tool has built our business around the skilled trades, and we believe America grows when the trades grow,” said Shane Moll, group president of Milwaukee Tool. “Joining the Alliance gives us another opportunity to build on the work we’ve been doing alongside the organizations that train and support the next generation of skilled tradespeople. We’re proud to bring those relationships, our experience and our continued investment to this effort.”
Milwaukee Tool supports more than 16,000 apprentices annually who are actively enrolled in skilled trades programs, working alongside more than 1,300 training centers and 25 national union and non-union partners across the United States. That work is grounded in longstanding relationships with organizations throughout the skilled trades.
Milwaukee Tool’s commitment to the skilled trades is part of the company’s broader investment in the United States. Over the past decade, Milwaukee Tool has invested more than $2 billion in its U.S. operations and added more than 4,000 American jobs in the past five years. All Milwaukee Tool global innovation originates at the company’s headquarters in Brookfield, Wisconsin, where it leads the development of solutions for professional tradespeople worldwide. Today, Milwaukee Tool employs more than 11,000 people nationwide and operates 34 facilities across the United States, spanning manufacturing, research and development, engineering, distribution, service and corporate operations.
Milwaukee Tool also sponsors T&D World 's Lineworker Focus and Faces of the Future departments by sending tool packages to the featured lineworkers.
If you are a lineworker and would like to participate, please send a photo of yourself working out in the field, by your bucket truck or competing at the International Lineman's Rodeo to Amy Fischbach . You can also fill out forms for Faces of the Future (for apprentices) or Lineworker Focus (for journeymen lineworkers).
You can also participate in a drawing at the T&D World booth at the International Lineman's Expo for a Milwaukee Tool prize package worth $1,348.85. Swing by the T&D World booth to get your badge scanned and enter the drawing. The winner will be announced at the Lineman's BBQ, and the prize will be shipped to the winner.
The Milwaukee Tool prize pack includes an assortment of pliers and screwdrivers manufactured in the United States as well as the M18 REDLITHIUM FORGE XC8.0 Battery, the M18 Dual Bay Simultaneous Super Charger and the M18 FUEL 7/16-in. Hex Utility HTIW w/ ONE-KEY Kit.

articles.content_orig:
Ashlyn Maddox, Eric Graise, Bonino, and more star in the world premiere musical version of Paul Gallico's 1940 novella.
October 02, 2026 By Andrew Gans, Logan Culwell-Block
Goodspeed Musicals' world premiere of The Snow Goose is currently playing the East Haddam, Connecticut, venue through October 18. Watch Ally Bonino sing "The World Don't Want to Know" from the new musical, which began performances August 28, in the video above.
Adapted from Paul Gallico 's 1940 novella, the musical was 
commissioned by the Goodspeed, and is written by Jonathan Larson Grant 
winners Scott Gilmour and McKenzie. Marshall Pailet ( Private Jones )
 is directing. The story follows a young man and woman who together 
rescue a wounded snow goose on the coast of England in the months before
 World War II, spawning a transformative friendship as the boy sets off 
to save soldiers trapped at Dunkirk.
The cast features Eric Graise ( Tracker , Step Up: High Water ) as Philip Rhayader, Ashlyn Maddox ( Parade ) as Frith, Sam Sherwood as The Bard, Charlie Webb ( Parade , The Notebook ) as Wilf, and Bonino ( Suffs ) as Harper. The ensemble comprises Alan Chandler, David Aron Damane ( The Queen of Versailles ), Matthew Davies, Leah Hofmann ( Mrs. Doubtfire ), Kiersten Kelly ( Jurassic World: Chaos Theory ), Amy Hillner Larsen ( Once Upon a One More Time ), Sophia Anna O'Brien, Gabriel Marcus Omlor, Ayanna Nicole Thomas ( Harry Potter and the Cursed Child , How To Dance in Ohio ),
 Patrick Tombs, and John Viggiano, with swings Sam Hoffman and Eleni Kontzamanys rounding out the company. Casting is by Geoff Josselson Casting.
Below, watch highlights from three other songs: Graise singing "I Owe It to Myself," the company performing "I Come Back to You," and Maddox singing "That Were Some Day."
The musical also has choreography by Misha Shields , music 
direction by Adam Souza, puppet design by Nicholas Mahon, scenic design 
by Emmie Finckel , costume design by Mallory Kay Nelson, lighting design 
by Aja M. Jackson , sound design by Jay Hilton, and wig, hair, and 
make-up design by J. Jared Janas and Cassie J. Williams. Chris Zaccardi serves as production stage manager, with Talleri A. McRae as access 
consultant and Emily Reutlinger as associate director.
Tickets are available at Goodspeed.org .

articles.title_orig: Spain’s government dealt a blow after parliament rejects housing measures amid protests
articles.title_zh: Spain’s government dealt a blow after parliament rejects housing measures amid protests
articles.content_orig:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez looks increasingly likely to call a snap election as early as Nov. 29 after the defeat of two key housing decrees in parliament on Friday.
Sánchez’s government unveiled the bills Tuesday to curb speculative practices, extend eviction protections for vulnerable tenants until 2030 and automatically renew existing rental contracts, following nationwide demonstrations after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal’s eviction from the apartment in which she had lived since 1956.
There initially appeared to be enough parliamentary support to pass at least one decree. But late on Thursday, the Catalan separatist Junts party, which defends landlords’ rights, announced it would oppose both measures, ensuring their defeat.
Sánchez responded defiantly to Junts’ move, saying on X he would not withdraw the decrees and casting the parliamentary vote as a breaking point : “The hour of truth has arrived,” he wrote, adding that lawmakers were obliged to cast “votes that will define them for generations to come.”
Ahead of the parliamentary session, government sources told Spanish newspaper El País that Sánchez was leaning toward calling a snap election. In an interview with Cadena SER, Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz said she had spoken with Sánchez and declined to rule out an early vote.
Spain’s current legislative term is due to end next summer , and speculation has been mounting that the prime minister — who is under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta , as well as corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies — could seek an opportune moment to call a snap election.
With housing consistently ranking among Spaniards’ top concerns, Sánchez now looks set to try to capitalize on popular discontent by casting the opposition as an obstacle to addressing the crisis.
The center-right People’s Party leads in electoral polls , with 34% support. Its potential partner, the far-right Vox party, is polling at 18%. Both oppose measures that challenge landlords’ property rights and instead favor deregulation and incentives for private owners.
At the request of Sánchez’s Socialist Party and far-left Sumar, which make up Spain’s coalition government, Friday’s vote was conducted by a show of hands, forcing lawmakers to publicly reveal their positions on the government’s housing measures.
Friday’s parliamentary vote came amid nationwide demonstrations over the housing crisis, with protest encampments in major Spanish cities. As the session began, protesters in Madrid marched toward the parliament, where they were met by more than 1,000 national police officers protecting the building.
The Spanish Tenants’ Union, which is leading the protests, is calling for a general strike and vowing to continue occupying the capital’s central Puerta del Sol square until their demands are met.
Spain’s national government has so far declined a request from Madrid’s local and regional governments to clear the square. Center-right regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso has filed suit in court demanding Sánchez’s government be ordered to clear the protest in Madrid; a ruling is expected this afternoon.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Reports First Combat Use of Its Own Ballistic Missile
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Reports First Combat Use of Its Own Ballistic Missile
articles.content_orig:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy hails use of FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which manufacturer says is being developed as an interceptor. What we know on day 1,682
Ukraine used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for ⁠the first time, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . Writing on Telegram on Thursday, the Ukrainian president said: “First combat use. Thank you for ⁠the result. Next – production.” He did not say where or how the FP-7 had been used. The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme, called Freyja, launched this year. Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km (125 miles), likening it to the US army Tactical Missile System but much cheaper. Ukraine – whose missile production is well behind Russia’s – has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element of its response to Russia’s frequent use of them in its attacks.
Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and an important bridge over the Dnipro River on Thursday , triggering fires ⁠in the capital, officials said. The ⁠school was struck early ​in the morning, but all the students were in a shelter and no injuries were reported, city authorities said. As Russian forces engaged in almost non-stop attacks on the city, Mayor Vitali ⁠Klitschko said two drones hit the Southern Bridge around noon. A new strike late in the evening damaged a support, part of the road surface and protective structures around the metro crossing the bridge. On Wednesday, Russian forces unleashed what Ukrainian officials described as the start of a cold-weather strike campaign against Ukraine’s power grid.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump , who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. He added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Ukraine ⁠also attacked the ⁠Russian ⁠city of Volgograd, ​home to a ⁠large oil refinery, with ⁠drones targeting ​industrial ‌facilities, ‌Governor Andrei Bocharov ‌said on Telegram on Friday. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity , according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
Europe has become increasingly dependent ‌on US fuel after banning Russian imports because of the war and after the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted supplies from the Middle East. The Trump administration has told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease soaring ⁠global fuel prices or face a ⁠potential US diesel export ban, according ​to three people close to the discussions.
At a Group of 20 meeting this week, trade ministers agreed it was “not acceptable” for countries to target food supplies in conflicts , France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier said on Thursday, adding that European leaders took aim at Russia on the issue. Forissier’s comments come as trade ministers from the G20 met for a second day in the midwestern US city of Milwaukee, where European officials criticised Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s grain sector. Forissier said European leaders’ comments against “the aggression of Russia in Ukraine” on food exports merely constituted “the truth”.
Moscow warned Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad , a Russian exclave and seaport located on the Baltic Sea, should any members of the military alliance try to cut it off. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”. Asked on Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with Nato or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.”
Putin said also on Thursday Russian assets of western companies that Moscow had seized could be returned in a “favourable scenario” . Last month, the Russian president ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro. He also said Russia ⁠would prefer to ⁠end ​the conflict ‌in ‌Ukraine through ‌talks and wanted Ukraine to be ‌a neutral country after ​the end of hostilities.

articles.title_orig: Another 'disturbing' botched execution. How does this happen?
articles.title_zh: Another 'disturbing' botched execution. How does this happen?
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
Christa Pike, sentenced to death in the 1995 murder of a Florida young woman, survived 2 syringes of lethal injection chemicals, her attorneys said.
Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike marks the latest in the country's long history of botched lethal injections.
Since 1982, there have been at least 64 botched executions, the vast majority of which involved lethal injection, according to an analysis by the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center. Seven of those execution attempts failed entirely because officials in Tennessee, Idaho, Alabama and Ohio could not properly insert intravenous lines.
Christa Pike in an April 2008 photo. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture slaying of Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Knoxville Job Corps student.
It's too soon to know for sure what went wrong when Tennessee tried to execute Christa Pike, but lethal injections have a long history of logistical and ethical issues that often resurface when an execution fails. Finding qualified medical professionals can be a struggle, as well as obtaining the drugs needed to carry out the execution.
Pharmaceutical manufacturers have increasingly sought to prevent their drugs from being used in executions, forcing states to seek alternative suppliers, including compounding pharmacies. Tennessee's previous supplier was a Texas compounding pharmacy that had been fined for failing to disclose a misdemeanor charge against an owner, according to a 2022 Tennessean investigation.
"Well-trained medical personnel generally do not want to be involved in executions, because they've taken an oath to do no harm," Ngozi Ndulue, deputy director of the Death Penalty Information Center, previously told the USA Today Network. "So we shouldn't be surprised when people without proper training are not able to successfully complete these IV insertions without going to fairly extreme measures."
Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution on Sept. 30.
In remarks the morning of Oct. 1, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said the failed execution was "deeply disturbing."
Pike was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 murder of her romantic rival, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. After Pike received two syringes filled with lethal injection chemicals, she was still alive and experiencing "unnecessary agony," her attorneys said in an emergency motion filed in the Tennessee Supreme Court to immediately stop the process.
"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy," Pike's attorneys said in a statement to USA Today.
Lethal injection is the most common execution method in the United States, and the most commonly botched, experts who study the death penalty say.
While several inmates have recently survived after executioners failed to access their veins, if Pike survived after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, it would be virtually unprecedented, according to Fordham University law professor Deborah Denno. Denno could recall just one other similar case: Florida teenager Willie Francis, who survived after being electrocuted in an electric chair in 1946.
"It's quite extraordinary that in 'modern times' that this would be happening," she said.
Injection problems stretch all the way back to the country's first lethal injection in 1982, when executioners in Texas struggled to find a suitable vein in Charles Brooks because of his heavy drug use, Denno wrote in a chapter of "The Elgar Companion to Capital Punishment and Society."
Factors including dehydration, stress, room temperature and certain medical conditions can also make veins more difficult to access. Another problem may be that the person inserting the IV line during an execution lacks experience, Denno, the founding director of the university's Neuroscience and Law Center, previously told USA Today.
"They may not be the person who you and I might go to to have blood drawn who's done this a thousand times, right?" she said. "I mean it may be somebody who is doing much lower level kind of work even though they're a medical professional."
During a failed execution in May, Dr. Mark Fowler unsuccessfully attempted to place a central line into Tennessee death row prisoner Tony Carruthers. Fowler had not placed a central line in at least 13 years, according to his deposition in litigation over Tennessee's execution procedures. Fowler testified that he had placed about a dozen central lines during his career and had no current hospital privileges.
While death row inmates aren't guaranteed a painless death, the U.S. Constitution mandates that their executions be free of "cruel and unusual punishment." In many cases, executions have proceeded despite injection issues, leading to some apparently gruesome deaths.
In 1988, minutes after lethal drugs began flowing into Texas inmate Raymond Landry's arms, a vein "blowout" caused a syringe to pop out and spray the chemicals across the execution chamber, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The execution team was ordered to reinsert the catheter, and Landry was pronounced dead 40 minutes after he was first strapped to the gurney.
Florida inmate Angel Diaz survived for 34 minutes after receiving two doses of lethal drugs in 2006, according to the center. An autopsy report found that the IV catheters had pierced through Diaz’s veins, and the deadly chemicals had been injected into soft tissue. Autopsy photos released by the New Republic in 2014 showed Diaz suffered severe chemical burns as a result.
Oklahoma prison staff attempting to execute inmate Clayton Lockett in 2014 failed to realize that lethal drugs were not going directly into his vein until he raised his head and started to make sounds, according to an official report. As officials scrambled to determine next steps, the drugs pooled under his skin in a swollen area larger than a golf ball and began to gradually kill him, the report said.
Denno said Pike could have survived because the lethal drugs weren't properly injected, calling executions a "negligent, sloppy process."
"The fact that they administered two doses is some indication that she wasn't receiving the medication," she said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed its execution protocol after which no additional procedures were permitted. Pike remained alive and was transported to a hospital on Sept. 30. The state has not released an update on Pike's condition as of Oct. 1.
Denno said there may also have been issues with the drug Pike was given.
An independent investigation previously found Tennessee's department of corrections failed to consistently test lethal injection drugs for potency, purity and contaminants, systemic failures stretching back years. The failures raised the likelihood that prisoners had been executed using expired, compromised or untested drugs.
The findings prompted Tennessee to overhaul its execution procedures. But the 44-page protocol released to The Tennessean in January 2025 contained significantly less detail about how execution drugs would be obtained, tested and stored than the state's previous 99-page protocol.
The Tennessee Department of Corrections has not publicly disclosed whether the drug used on Sept. 30 was compounded. Compounded drugs are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration, meaning the agency does not verify their "safety, effectiveness or quality."
"We don't know whether that drug was expired ... it may not have the right chemical balance," Denno said.
Contributing: Jimmy Jenkins, Arizona Republic; Kelly Puente and Evan Mealins, Nashville Tennessean; Gregg Zoroya, USA TODAY

articles.title_orig: Fighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fears Further of All-Out War
articles.title_zh: Fighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fears Further of All-Out War
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.
Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the frontlines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.
Still, there are few signs that the Saudi-backed government intends to begin a serious counteroffensive against the Houthis in the near future, despite the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi calling for a general mobilisation against the rebels on September 25.
The government instead seems to be pursuing a more gradual process, building up its military forces and attempting to make them more cohesive.
Abdul Basir al-Bahr, a senior official with the internationally recognised government army’s Taiz Military Axis, told Al Jazeera that the general mobilisation call was part of that effort.
Al-Bahr said plans include bringing reserve personnel back into the military’s ranks and retraining them, alongside local anti-Houthi fighters and civilian volunteers.
He stressed that the measures were at an early stage and their battlefield impact could not be judged yet.
In Taiz, Al Jazeera’s field monitoring has found that fighting has continued since early September without any major shifts that can be directly attributed to the general mobilisation.
The picture is similar on other fronts, including the Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and in Lahj, south of Taiz.
Yemeni government field commanders told Al Jazeera the general mobilisation had not yet led to frontline reinforcements.
But that does not mean that military activity has not intensified. On Monday, Colonel Majid al-Nazili, spokesman for the government’s military forces, said the forces had carried out more than 400 strikes over a 24-hour period against the Houthis, causing losses in personnel and equipment.
The ability of the Yemeni government’s military to halt further Houthi advances since the Red Sea reversal appears to reflect a combination of more favourable defensive terrain in the Taiz mountains and Lahj, as well as increased firepower.
The loss of the coastline was aided by weak coordination among anti-Houthi forces, who – despite officially being under one military chain of command – appeared divided and unable to respond quickly to the Houthi advance.
In both Taiz and Lahj – as well as Marib in Yemen’s north – anti-Houthi forces have shown more unity and have years of experience preventing Houthi military advances. Government-aligned forces have also had time to reinforce areas where the Houthis are attempting to advance.
The use of air power is also growing, with government forces reporting hundreds of air, drone, artillery and other strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements in the past few days.
After having seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, the Houthis now need control of the mountainous high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and the roads leading inland to consolidate those gains. Their attempts to take that high ground have so far failed, while the expanded territory has increased the manpower and logistical burden of defending their new positions.
The result, so far, is increasingly a battle over roads and supply lines, with neither side so far able to reproduce the kind of rapid breakthrough seen on the Red Sea coast.
Al Jazeera’s Yemen Editor, Ahmed al-Shalafi, said that the current Houthi attack on Taiz was the result of the group’s desire to secure its coastal gains, as well as an attempt to separate government forces.
He attributed their lack of success so far to a number of reasons.
“When you are talking about Taiz, you’re not just talking about Taiz itself, Taiz is connected to Lahj, Aden, Hodeidah, it has political importance, geographical importance, military importance,” al-Shalafi said.
“There is a difference between the Houthis entering Mocha and between them entering Taiz [city],” he added. “Firstly, the front is strong, there is a cohesion between the tribes and the local forces and the government forces … Secondly, the Houthis do not have a strong base of support in Taiz.”
