articles.title_orig: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.title_zh: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.content_orig:
Environmental Law and Climate Policy Insights
Last week, about halfway down the New York Times’ Monday morning newsletter, there was a video titled “ Living Next to Mexico’s Toxic Reservoir .”  I watched it, appalled not only by the dangerous conditions described in the video and accompanying article , but also by the fact that I had never heard of this enormous environmental justice disaster.  I worried that if I—someone who inevitably spends some part of everyday thinking about environmental injustices—was previously unaware that over 20,000 people have been forced to live around a toxic reservoir for approximately five decades , then it was unlikely that these communities had been receiving much, if any, attention and support from environmental organizations outside of the region.  It turns out that, unfortunately, my concern was well-founded.  In 2023, Judges for the Society of Environmental Journalists’ 22nd Annual Awards for Reporting on the Environment awarded “ Los Olvidados de Hidalgo ” [English transcript here ]—a N+ Focus feature story about the Endhó Dam—third place, in part because of how “shockingly unknown” the story was.
The Endhó Dam was built in the 1950s as a freshwater reservoir, and for about 20 years, it served as such.  There was plenty of clean water to irrigate the crops in the otherwise arid Mezquital Valley, and the dam provided locals with an enjoyable and clean natural environment .  In the 1970s, however, as the population of Mexico City continued to grow, federal officials decided to begin diverting the capital’s storm runoff and wastewater into the dam.  This means that for the past 50 years, all of the wastewater from a metropolitan area of around 20 million people has been dumped into the Endhó Dam.  Every year, the dam receives around 326 million cubic meters of largely untreated wastewater—that’s enough wastewater to fill over 130,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Approximately 60% of the wastewater does pass through a treatment plant, but before the treated water can make it to the reservoir, it mixes with discharge and waste from a nearby oil refinery, thermopower plant, and the rest of the massive industrial corridor that surrounds the dam.  The result is an environmental and public health nightmare, referred to by locals as “ Mexico’s toilet bowl ,” and “the world’s largest cesspool.”
Yury Uribe, a lifelong resident of the region and activist with El Movimiento Social por la Tierra, has been organizing her community in an attempt to get the Mexican government to recognize the Endhó Dam as an environmental emergency, but through no fault of her own, she has seen little success.  Although the area was declared an ecological restoration zone in 2024, the declaration did not allocate any funding to cleaning up the area.  Accordingly, Endhó Dam residents continue to suffer from seemingly endless environmental and health problems.  Cancer rates in the area tripled between 2007­–2018, and today,
communities surrounding the dam report rates of cancer and kidney failures that are sometimes double the national average ; the dam contaminates the surrounding towns’ wells —the main source of drinking water for those towns’ residents; and the hyacinth that grows on top of the dam has become a breeding ground for mosquitos , endangering locals’ livestock and forcing residents to “ lock themselves inside ” every evening.  Emiliano Rodríguez Mega, a long-time science reporter covering Latin America and the NYT reporter who covered this story, said that even he “ had never quite seen something like the Endhó Dam .”
The big question that normally follows learning about an injustice like this is, “how is this allowed to happen?”  Unfortunately, the answer this time is the same as it almost always is:  some communities—low-income, marginalized communities—are seen as expendable.  As explained by the legendary environmental justice advocates Dr. Robert Bullard and Beverly Wright, the people and communities who are viewed as being expendable suffer from having “ the wrong complexion for protection .”
Areas like the Endhó Dam are often referred to as “ sacrifice zones ” because “the health and safety of people in these communities is being effectively sacrificed for the economic gains and prosperity of others.”  In this instance, the low-income farming communities living around the dam ( a substantial percentage of whom are Indigenous , primarily from the Otomí Nation ) are being sacrificed to protect Mexico City from flooding and to keep the profitable agricultural area surrounding the Tula River rich with nutrients.  Similar cases of environmental injustice and racism exist around the world:  the risk of cancer to the primarily Black residents of “Cancer Alley” in Louisiana is over 50 times higher than the national average; 95% of children in Kabwe, Zambia , largely from poor families, have dangerously elevated levels of lead in their blood caused by the nearby lead mining; nearly every Aamjiwnaang First Nation household living in Canada’s “Chemical Valley” suffers from high rates of miscarriages, asthma, and cancer.  The examples, unfortunately, abound.  Recognizing that these areas “illustrat[e] egregious human rights violations, particularly of poor, vulnerable and marginalized communities,” former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment, David Boyd, described sacrifice zones as “ the worst imaginable dereliction of a State’s obligation to respect, protect, and fulfil[l] the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.”
How do we finally rid the world of a system in which, as Naomi Klein put it in This Changes Everything , “poisoning [whole subsets of humanity] in the name of progress [is] somehow acceptable”?  Like most things worth doing, it’s somewhat complicated.  But as the Climate Justice Alliance—an alliance of over 100 frontline communities in the climate justice movement— has noted , it is critically necessary not only because everyone has a right to drink clean water and breathe clean air, but also because “[o]ur society cannot build a more just and healthy economy if communities continue to be seen as expendable.”  Eliminating sacrifice zones can be distilled into a three-stage process:  (1) prioritize protecting the communities living in sacrifice zones from further harm; (2) allocate resources to repairing the harm that has already been done and passing strong regulations; and (3) invest in the communities that have historically been viewed as expendable, and ensure that they have power over their own futures.  Let’s get to work.

articles.title_orig: Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
articles.title_zh: Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
articles.content_orig:
Pike alive but in critical condition as experts call ordeal that unfolded in Tennessee ‘unimaginably barbaric’
Top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community are calling for a moratorium on the US death penalty after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike left the prisoner alive but in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care.
The recent spate of harrowingly botched executions across US death penalty states reached a new low late on Wednesday when Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, called off the procedure after Pike had been injected with two full syringes of pentobarbital. She is the only person to have survived being administered 5g of the sedative – a massive dose that under normal circumstances is considered fatal.
An hour after the first injection was given, she was overheard by eyewitnesses to be still breathing, choking and struggling, and was found to have a heartbeat. Her lawyers said that her current condition, and the degree to which she may have been brain-damaged through oxygen deprivation, were as yet unknown.
Sandra Babcock, a death penalty scholar at Cornell law school who advises Pike’s legal team, told the Guardian that the events that unfolded were “unimaginably barbaric. They demand accountability.”
She added that at a minimum Lee must now “commute Christa Pike’s death sentence to life imprisonment”.
Another of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, who was present in the death chamber, called Pike’s ordeal “cruel and torturous”. He said he had personally counted seven needles stuck in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of a teenage classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Leading voices on the death penalty in America told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings had to be halted. Bryan Stevenson, an internationally renowned death penalty lawyer and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative in Montgomery, Alabama, said that many warnings had been made in recent months that US executions were flawed and unreliable.
“Nearly a dozen botched executions in recent years should have suspended executions long before now,” he said.
Stevenson said it was time to turn around the threshold question. Instead of asking whether a prisoner deserved to die for the crime committed, the question should be: “Do our governments which tolerate inequality, unreliability and bias deserve to kill?”
He added: “Last night’s tragedy makes clear we should stop the misguided policy of killing people to show that killing is wrong.”
Wednesday night was the second time in five months that Tennessee had failed to carry out an execution. In May, Tony Carruthers survived the death chamber after the execution team were unable to set up an IV line.
He has been given a new execution date for next May.
That followed Alabama, which also failed to execute two death row prisoners, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith , having been unable to find a vein. The spectacle of prisoners being sent to their deaths, only to have the executions called off as a result of basic failures in IV procedures, has sent death penalty states scrambling to find alternatives to lethal injections.
In turn, those alternative procedures have become mired in complications and disputes. Miller and Smith were both eventually killed by Alabama using an experimental procedure, nitrogen gas, that veterinarians have banned as inhumane for the euthanasia of cats and dogs.
In June, a federal judge blocked Alabama’s use of nitrogen in executions, ruling it cruel and unusual punishment.
Other states have opted for the firing squad. But recent firing squad executions have been troubled by bullets missing the heart , to the extent that the suggestion has been raised that some of the mis-targeted shots may have been intentional.
Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America after her book Dead Man Walking was turned into a film of the same name, told the Guardian that the events on Wednesday night were the definition of cruelty.
“This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her. She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”
Prejean added that she hoped the agony Pike had endured “would be redemptive for others, and help to wake up the nation”.
As the number of gruesome botched lethal injections rapidly mounts, the central premise that has been held up by supporters – that it is a humane, medicalised and scientific way to kill a person – has come under fire. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta, Georgia, who has reviewed hundreds of autopsies of executed people in the US, said that lethal injections would never deserve the label of medicine.
“This is the impersonation of a medical act. It is the theft of a medical act. So when it goes awry, that is not at all surprising to me.”
Zivot was invited to present as an expert witness at a hearing convened in August by a special master in the Pike case. He warned the senior judge that Pike had a blood condition in which her blood platelets were elevated that rendered her vulnerable to blood clots.
Zivot told the hearing that Pike, as a small woman who had been in solitary confinement on death row for almost 30 years, probably had veins that were of poor quality, small in caliber, and hard to find. “I told them. I warned them,” he said.
The special master rejected almost all the evidence presented to him.
The last time that the US saw a moratorium on executions was in 1972 when the supreme court ruled in Furman v Georgia that capital punishment was capricious and arbitrary in its rendition. The ban was lifted four years later.
Paradoxically, calls for a renewed nationwide pause are reaching fever pitch at precisely the time that pressure to carry out executions is also peaking. Donald Trump has repeatedly exhorted death penalty states and the federal Department of Justice to speed up judicial killings, and his orders are having an effect.
Last year saw the highest number of US executions – 47 across 12 states – in 16 years.
Prejean said that the answer to the growing determination of Trump and the death penalty states to carry out executions was to bring the American people closer to the action. She pointed to Gallup’s findings tracking popular sentiment towards capital punishment.
In 1993, when her book came out, 80% of Americans supported the death penalty for convicted murderers. Now that figure is 52%.
“That’s progress, though not enough. People have good hearts, but they are too removed from the process that is secret and hidden. We have got to bring this to the people, bring them into the execution chamber, so that they too become a witness.”

articles.title_orig: 2026 Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series | Race #3 | Suzuka Circuit | Preview
articles.title_zh: 2026 Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series | Race #3 | Suzuka Circuit | Preview
articles.content_orig:
October 2nd, 2026 by Justin Melillo
The Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series continues this Saturday, October 3rd, featuring 32 of the best sim racers around the globe. Next up, the competition heads to Suzuka Circuit in Japan for the third round of the five-round season.
Another two names were added to the winner’s list after Silverstone last week in Diogo Pinto and Dayne Warren. Once again, two drivers from the Red Bull / Verstappen camp and the Coanda camp, respectively, as they joined Florian Lebigre and Charlie Collins who won in the opening round. Will it be another split at Suzuka, or can one team take full control?
Live streaming of the events will begin on Saturday at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .
Diogo Pinto, Dayne Warren score victories at Silverstone | Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship
The biggest action from Silverstone came in qualifying and in the battle for eighth in the Sprint. Diogo Pinto just took the pole position over Alejandro Sánchez, which allowed for him to take the lead on the start and go on to win the Sprint. Behind that, Cooper Webster qualified in eighth, and was on track to finish there, but managed to pass Dayne Warren for seventh before the checkers. That wound up putting Warren in first for the Main, and Warren would go on to win after 30 minutes.
There have been seven prior seasons of the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series, but never in those previous 64 races has there been a trip to Japan to take on the twists and turns of Suzuka International Racing Course.
One of the world’s truly great race tracks, Suzuka has been the home of the Japanese Grand Prix since the 1980s and its flowing layout regularly puts the circuit at or near the top of the list of most Formula One drivers’ favorites. As if that weren’t enough, Suzuka boats three different configurations – Suzuka East, Suzuka West and Suzuka Full, the latter two featuring a rare figure eight layout where the back straightaway crosses the front section track on an overpass.
Designed by noted circuit architect John Hugenholtz (who also designed the original Zandvoort circuit), Suzuka opened in 1962 and served primarily as a test track for Honda and as the site of sports car racing including the Suzuka 1000K and the 8 Hours of Suzuka and MotoGP motorcycle events. Suzuka was nominated to stage the Japanese Grand Prix in 1987 and has often been the site of the Formula One season finale. As such, Suzuka has been the decisive event in some of the closest battles for the World Championship of Drivers and has witnessed a number of controversial incidents, including clashes between Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost. Suzuka also hosted non-championship NASCAR races in 1996 and ’97.
In addition to its signature crossover layout, Suzuka features a number of notable challenges including a testing series of esses, the multi-apex Spoon Curve and dauntingly fast 130R corner. The race track also serves as the foundation for a major sports and entertainment facility including an amusement park whose giant Ferris Wheel is prominent in photographs and television images of the circuit.
After Suzuka, the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship heads to the Autódromo José Carlos Pace, or Interlagos for short, for the fourth round of the season. The events are scheduled for Saturday, October 10th, and will be live starting at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .
For more information on the 2026 Porsche Esports Supercup season, visit www.iracing.com/pesc . For more information on iRacing and for special offers, visit www.iracing.com .

Crude oil prices are set for a modest weekly decline today, as reports of a strong rebound in oil flows out of the Persian Gulf trumped news of more U.S. troops moving to the Middle East and China’s Thursday decision to halt fuel exports this month.
At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $102.24 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $92.62. Both benchmarks posted strong gains in September and while the start to October has been lower, if hostilities in the Persian Gulf escalate again, the upward potential will return.
“The market is taking stock of a distinctly mixed set of signals this week,” Reuters quoted KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer as saying. “A healthier-looking Saudi export picture is being offset by reports of another US aircraft carrier heading toward the Gulf and by China’s decision to curb refined product exports,” Waterer also said.
“The US-Israeli war on Iran is difficult to predict. In our base case, we model early November, following the US midterm elections, as the main scenario for an easing of the conflict,” said David Doherty, Head of Natural Resources at BNEF earlier this week.
“However, we think it is highly likely that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the US blockade of Iran will persist in some form into the new year. The longer the disruption lasts, the longer it will take for flows to return to normal,” Doherty also said.
The likelihood of the war extending into next year indeed looks quite substantial. President Trump’s latest remarks on Iran support that scenario. “Now I have to make a decision. They'll ‌either sign a very fair deal, or they won't exist any longer,” Trump told the media earlier this week following a report by the Wall Street Journal about a third aircraft carrier en route to the Middle East plus some 10,000 troops.

articles.title_orig: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.title_zh: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Wilhelm 02 October 2026
Would it really be a prospective student visit without a free t-shirt? If you see a student walking backwards across campus giving a Taylor tour, you’re bound to see some visitors with classic Taylor purple t-shirts hanging over their arms. However, you might not know that this common prospective student gift is creating uncommon change in the lives of Guatemalan families through Taylor’s partnership with World Orphans .
World Orphans is a non-profit organization with a vision of relational healing and financial independence for families who have been separated due to poverty or abuse. One of the ministry arms within the organization is the World Orphans Market , an economic empowerment program. This program equips women with sewing skills, and these women are then employed as artisans to return to them the dignity of meaningful work and financial freedom. All of World Orphans’ work is grounded in a Christ-centered philosophy of human worth: everyone is created with intrinsic dignity and with a God-given purpose. Additionally, World Orphans works through local churches, ensuring that these women are supported by Christ-centered communities as they work their way out of poverty and towards better lives for their families.
Like so many Taylor stories, Taylor’s journey to partnering with World Orphans is a story of community. When the Admissions team connected with World Orphans, they saw an opportunity—an opportunity for Taylor as an organization to model the same mission it seeks to foster in its student body. Taylor always has a need for t-shirts—particularly in Admissions. Here, Taylor’s tangible need for shirts meets these Guatemalan women’s tangible need for living-wage work, creating a true, mutually beneficial partnership.
As the Admissions team collaborated with World Orphans’ Guatemalan team, they encountered some community connections that made one thing clear—God had already been opening doors for this partnership. One of these connections was Lily Sachsenmeier ’26, who finished her Orphaned & Vulnerable Children degree interning at World Orphans in Guatemala, where "a highlight was getting to talk with social workers at World Orphans who support local families, empowering parents with education and resources to care for their children. I was really moved by the personal experiences they shared and by their passion for their work."
During her time in Guatemala, Sachsenmeier also had the opportunity to meet some of the artisans making the t-shirts for Taylor Admissions, bringing this community story full circle.
Reflecting on Taylor’s choosing World Orphans to supply their next batch of Admissions t-shirts, Sachsenmeier said, "I’m deeply touched that Taylor is partnering with World Orphans. As a student, I got many free t-shirts for events and programs, and I’m so glad that Taylor is being intentional about where they source some of these t-shirts. I’m incredibly proud that Taylor is investing in t-shirts made by these women in Guatemala as part of World Orphans’ economic empowerment program!"
At Taylor, a t-shirt is so much more than a clothing item—it’s a walking billboard for who we are. It says, "I believe in what goes on here." Now, Taylor purple has additional purpose. These t-shirts are a physical manifestation of our mission to "minister Christ’s redemptive love, grace, and truth to a world in need." They are a reminder of a God who opens doors. And a reminder of what a true partnership can look like.
Learn more about how Taylor equips students to break cycles of vulnerability through our Orphaned & Vulnerable Children major.

articles.title_orig: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.title_zh: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.content_orig:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV) - Logan and Kenzie Mendonca, a brother and sister from McMinnville, are competing in karate tournaments around the world.
“We are more stressed watching each other fight than when we are competing ourselves,” Kenzie said.
The siblings have traveled to multiple countries to compete.
“Canada, Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Paraguay, Costa Rica,” Logan said.
“I think Africa, just to make one,” Logan said, referring to places they haven’t competed.
Logan and Kenzie recently returned from Guadalajara, Mexico, with Youth League Karate gold medals. Their medals hang in the family dojo, the Mendonca Academy of Martial Arts in McMinnville.
“It’s a place of calm. I come in here and my problems are outside,” Logan said.
The siblings have competed in karate since they were three years old. Their father, Tony, leads their training routine.
“You learn time management, you learn how to get your things done because the dojo isn’t something that you can skip. It is a mandatory part of your routine,” Kenzie said.
“Just traveling and seeing crazy stuff but also winning and losing together is something really special to me,” Logan said.
Logan and Kenzie competed at the Junior Pan American Karate Championships in San Jose, Costa Rica. Logan won the Junior Male title in his fifth appearance at the event.
“I went bronze, silver, silver, then I took fifth and this year I won, so this year was my first year winning, pulling it out. It was my third year in the finals,” Logan said.
Logan is ranked No. 1 in the U.S. and is a senior at McMinnville High School. Kenzie, a sophomore, won Pan American Cadet Female silver for a third straight year.
“I think the most-cocky part of it for me is being in three finals before Logan,” Kenzie said.
“Yeah, I mean her record is better than mine,” Logan said.
“On paper if you look at like our ages my stuff looks cooler than his,” Kenzie said. “Because I’m better earlier.”
Both Logan and Kenzie were named team captains for the United States. They will next compete at the Junior World Championships in Poland.
“He’s Spiderman but when he comes home, he’s Peter Parker,” Kenzie said.
Logan is a National Merit Scholar semifinalist with aspirations of attending college in France to study physics.
“Right now Peter Parker has national merit, but nobody knows he’s Spiderman and nobody cares,” Kenzie said.
Logan and Kenzie will miss about nine days of school for the trip to Poland. They are completing tests during lunch breaks and will bring homework with them.

articles.title_orig: Mid-Michigan musicians complete 60-hour-long jam session, breaking world record
articles.title_zh: Mid-Michigan musicians complete 60-hour-long jam session, breaking world record
articles.content_orig:
What makes a good jam session? Maybe it’s the combination of instruments or the vibe of the music.
For a group of Michigan musicians this week , they cared less about the quality and more about how long they could play for what they believe is a record-breaking jam session.
The world record attemp t started Monday at 10 a.m. with six musicians on stage at UrbanBeat in Old Town Lansing, Michigan. Jeff Boog helped organize the jam.
"We are doing a continuous musical collaboration for three days without doing what humans normally do, which is to stop and take a break, change the subject, go do something else," he said.
There's no official Guinness World Record for longest jam, so Boog and his friends settled on going beyond the longest nonstop improvised music session they could find: 57 hours played in Spain in 2024.
They set a few rules for themselves to make the challenge more structured: like having at least three musicians on stage at all times, keeping everything improvised with no planning ahead of time and, most importantly, the music never stopping.
But they weren’t going to do it alone, so they recruited more than a hundred other musicians, from professionals to amateurs to anyone who just wanted to play, to swap out in shifts for the marathon jam. There were guitars, clarinets, bongos and a tuba on stage at various points among other instruments.
By 7 p.m. on Tuesday, more than halfway through the jam, dozens of musicians had taken the stage, many of them meeting for the first time. One of them was singer and guitar player Mary McGuire.
"I think I just played with three different drummers, probably seven or eight guitar players, two different bass players," she said. "The piano player was great, and then a woman jumped up and was singing harmonies."
Another participant, Zachary Mead said collaborating like this isn’t as hard as you might think
"People that play music, they kind of just they figure it out," Mead said. "They start playing and then they figure it out."
With no way to really know how the jam would go before they started, organizer John K. Addis was happy to see how everyone had come together.
"They are jamming constantly. There are no covers, no pauses, and somehow it's all working," Addis said. "I don't think we've had a pause more than like five seconds."
The group crossed the 57 hour mark with a countdown Wednesday night, breaking the record set in Spain, but the music didn't stop just yet.
3 hours later at 10 p.m. and after 60 straight hours of playing, the musicians finally put down their instruments.
UrbanBeat owner Terry Terry, who had hopped on stage a few times throughout the jam to play flute and percussion, made this declaration:
"We set out to prove that Lansing is the music capital of Michigan, and I think we're now the jam capital of the world," Terry said.
Organizers say they plan to submit their performance to Guinness with hopes that it will be officially recognized, and that they’re ready to come back if anyone else decides to jam out longer.
Additionally, the jam has inspired new ideas for the Lansing music scene including creating more dedicated nights for musicians who've never met to collaborate together.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been higher still if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.title_orig: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.title_zh: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title_orig: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.title_zh: 2026 Right Livelihood laureates challenge autocracy, patriarchy, and AI bias
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award is honoring women and women-led organisations confronting the world ’ s most entrenched power structures: authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence, and unchecked AI development.
Their common thread is resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the centre.
The 2026 Right Livelihood Award, also known as the “ Alternative Nobel Prize, ” has been awarded to Jalila Haider from Pakistan “ for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal,” the Rural Women ’ s Assembly “ for organising rural women across Southern Africa into a united force defending land, seed, and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession,” the Georgian Young Lawyers ’ Association “ for building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown,” and Timnit Gebru from the US “ for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency.”
World Council of Churches general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay commended the women honored. “ These Right Livelihood laureates exemplify the kind of empowerment that is life-flourishing, deep-rooted, and of the people,” he said, adding a special congratulations to the Rural Women ’ s Assembly from his home country of South Africa. “ I have seen firsthand the power of volunteers who can put the region ’ s food systems back into the hands of resilient people and communities.”
For over 45 years, the Right Livelihood Award has honoured and supported people leading the way to a just, peaceful, and sustainable world for all.
The 2026 awardees were chosen from 200 nominees from 72 countries. They will be honoured during a televised award presentation in Stockholm on 1 December.

articles.title_orig: World Number 979 Stuns All at Alfred Dunhill Links Championship
articles.title_zh: World Number 979 Stuns All at Alfred Dunhill Links Championship
articles.content_orig:
Michael Stewart arrived at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship with little of the attention surrounding the star names in the field. By the end of the opening round, the 36-year-old Scot had given everyone a reason to notice him.
Stewart, ranked 979th in the world, fired a seven-under 65 at Carnoustie to share the first-round lead with Australia's Jack Buchanan.
It was a striking result for a player who has made only five appearances on the main European circuit, with his most recent coming in 2023. Stewart was also operating on a quick turnaround. He had finished second in the Tartan Tour's Duddingston Classic less than 24 hours earlier before heading to the Dunhill Links on a sponsor's invitation.
Early in his round, there was little indication that something special was coming. Stewart managed just one birdie on the front nine.
USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
Then everything changed. An eagle at the par-five 12th sparked a remarkable stretch in which Stewart played the next five holes in six under. His putter suddenly caught fire, and a steady round turned into one that placed him above a field loaded with established names.
"It's easy to get yourself up for this event. I played Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday [at Duddingston], straight here," Stewart said. "I've played here a lot in the past and am just delighted to be part of the event.
"I grew up on a links course. I played nice all day to be honest. Lots of fairways, lots of greens and then on the back, the putter got hot."
Buchanan matched Stewart's seven-under total at Kingsbarns, while South Africans MJ Daffue and Casey Jarvis finished one stroke behind the leaders.
Matt Fitzpatrick, fresh from victory at the French Open, opened with a four-under 68 to sit three shots back. Five-time major champion Brooks Koepka carded a 69 at Carnoustie to reach three under, while Tommy Fleetwood finished another shot behind.
Defending champion Robert MacIntyre ended the day at one under, although his score became only part of the story.
MacIntyre became furious over a drone flying above him as he prepared to play the par-three eighth, his penultimate hole. Tournament officials later spoke with him following the incident.
"It drives me insane. I've had previous for it," MacIntyre said.
"I asked the rules official twice before the shot on the eighth about the drone. I can't say anything just now.
"He's obviously heard me swear a few times straight at the camera guy. We'll see what the TD [tournament director] has got to say."
MacIntyre wasn't the only player whose frustration became visible.
Tyrrell Hatton endured his own angry moment on the same par-three hole after catching a bunker shot thin and sending the ball through the green. Hatton repeatedly slammed his club into the sand, and Sky Sports' commentary team apologized to viewers following his reaction.
Hatton, playing alongside his father Jeff, eventually signed for a two-over 74.
Other notable returns and unusual moments marked the day. Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter made their first DP World Tour appearances since January 2023 after joining LIV Golf in 2022. Westwood finished at one under, while Poulter ended the round at level par.
Meanwhile, former Real Madrid and Wales footballer Gareth Bale supplied one of the strangest shots of the opening round. Playing the 17th at St Andrews in the team competition, Bale sent his ball onto the roof of the famous Jigger Inn.
Yet amid drones, flying clubs, returning LIV Golf players and a football star finding a pub roof, Stewart produced the performance that mattered most on the leaderboard.
Less than a day after competing on the Tartan Tour, the world No. 979 walked off Carnoustie tied for the lead in one of the DP World Tour's most recognizable events.
For Stewart, the equation was considerably simpler than everything happening around him: fairways, greens and, once he reached the back nine, a putter that suddenly refused to cool down.

articles.title_orig: Home Assistant renames Home Assistant Cloud to Link
articles.title_zh: Home Assistant renames Home Assistant Cloud to Link
articles.content_orig:
﻿Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.
﻿Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.
The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb — in name at least. “We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds,” founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today’s announcement . “Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out.”
The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and that’s what he’s looking to change.
I spoke with Schoutsen at the Z-Wave Summit in Boca Raton, Florida, this week about the changes and Home Assistant’s future plans, which include lowering barriers to entry by developing simpler dashboards, making setup more intuitive, and using generative AI to reduce complexity. He also said they plan to launch a new hub next year that’s more user-friendly. “We’re growing up.”
“You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.”
Renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Link is mostly symbolic. The features stay the same, aside from some back-end improvements to speed and reliability. The new name also tries to address a concern some new users had that it meant Home Assistant ran in the cloud, says Schoutsen. Home Assistant runs on local hardware and controls your smart home locally, but this means once you leave your home network, you can’t control anything.
For $6.50 a month or $65 a year, Home Assistant Link gives you a convenient way to access your Home Assistant instance from anywhere, alongside the option to enable other internet-dependent features such as integration with Alexa and Google voice control, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and encrypted backups.
The move addresses an awkward dynamic for the platform. Schoutsen and his team have spent years campaigning against proprietary cloud ecosystems, which he believes hurt the smart home, and encouraging people not to buy cloud-dependent products, all while offering a service with “cloud” in the name. However, unlike some cloud services, Home Assistant Cloud was never mandatory, and you could always replicate everything it provided with other methods; the same remains true for Link.
Schoutsen says Link is also different from many cloud services because it has no access to your data. Link is run by Nabu Casa , Home Assistant’s commercial partner, and all Link traffic is encrypted . “We can’t see it, and we don’t want to,“ he says. “You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” The service provides a revenue stream to fund the platform’s development, with 60 percent of the profit going to the non-profit Open Home Foundation that runs Home Assistant.
For Home Assistant, cloud-dependent products are a hard no. “The cloud is ruining how people think of the smart home,” says Schoutsen, pointing to the recent examples of Nest shutting off the cloud for its early thermostats , smart TVs sending your data to the cloud without you knowing, and Weber sunsetting the June Oven’s servers . “Now you have a dumb oven that cost $1,500. It’s crazy,” he says. “People get so used to it and get so disappointed by it.”
The cloud isn’t all bad, Schoutsen concedes. Speech-to-text, backups, and AI work better online, but the problem is products that stop working without it. He wants product manufacturers to commit to offering local control by default, using open standards (Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, ESPHome), never locking basic features behind a cloud, and allowing users to control their own data.
“I’d love to see a nutrition label on boxes showing if a product is cloud-dependent or not,” he says, adding that they’re building a database to help consumers find products that aren’t fully reliant on the cloud.
This stance against the cloud is likely to appeal to consumers who are increasingly concerned about who has access to their data. But Home Assistant still has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream. Schoutsen says Home Assistant is installed in an estimated 2.7 million homes, but that’s still a fraction of the reach of Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings , and Apple Home. Winning over mainstream users will be hard.
The biggest barrier to entry is complexity. Home Assistant does a lot, meaning you have a lot of choice, which can be overwhelming. “If you want to try something with Home Assistant, the answer is never no,” says Schoutsen. “We want everything to be possible, which means that the UX is more complicated, and that scares people.” In comparison, “You open Apple Home, and there’s like nothing you can do,” he says.
Over the last few years, the team has been working to remove those barriers without taking away functionality. “We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling,” he says. There are plans to launch a successor to the Home Assistant Green hub that will be easier to set up. “We want to make it more like onboarding a Philips Hue hub,” says Schoutsen.
They are also working to make the UX easier and will integrate the HACS community store — where users find and install community-built integrations — into Home Assistant next month. This should make integrations easier to find and set up. “If people haven’t tried Home Assistant in over a year, they should give it a shot,” he says.
“We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling.”
Another big push that could turn into a major selling point for the platform is a “No Device Left Behind” program . Nabu Casa is developing devices that will more easily bring people’s existing analog or legacy tech into the platform — such as old receivers, AC units, solar panel inverters, even TVs — using technology such as serial , IR, and Modbus .
Schoutsen sees AI as a big driver for Home Assistant. “AI is going to solve the complexity problem, and our biggest weakness is becoming our biggest strength,” he says. As a broad, open platform that can bring together data and controls from across your smart home, Home Assistant could provide a useful foundation for AI agents.
I used Claude to set up Home Assistant last year, and it was a big improvement over trying to figure out what on earth YAML was. “Soon you’re just going to have your agent configure your software for you,” he says. “Because people don’t want the software, they just want the solution that comes out of it.” Schoutsen acknowledges that agents raise obvious privacy concerns, but says Home Assistant keeps your data at home and you can choose which agent to trust with it, including one that runs locally.
Ultimately, Home Assistant may not need to reinvent itself to win over the mainstream if it can become the foundational layer that lets your home talk to your AI agent or platform of choice. “If you just have a box in your house that runs Home Assistant that connects all your data to your agents or to, say, Apple Home, that’s great,” he says. “That’s a win for Home Assistant.”

articles.title_orig: When teens get colorectal cancer, it’s often an aggressive form of the disease
articles.title_zh: When teens get colorectal cancer, it’s often an aggressive form of the disease
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Kennedy Center announces it’s moving its annual awards gala off site for the first time in its history amid battle over Trump’s planned renovations
Jo Henderson was 17 when she was diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer . It came after months of symptoms — stomach pain, bloating, constipation — and months of testing.
“I was expecting a gluten allergy, lactose intolerance,” said Henderson, now 18, of Seekonk, Massachusetts. “Literally anything but cancer.”
Colorectal cancer in people younger than 20 is exceptionally rare: People like Henderson are about one in a million , and account for fewer than 100 cases per year in the United States. But a new study found that most cases of colorectal cancer in kids and teenagers are aggressive, and often diagnosed at advanced stages.
The findings show that “the adolescent and the youngest of the young adults are at particular risk for bad outcomes and are a unique and vulnerable population even compared to people in their 30s and 40s,” said Dr. Danielle Cameron, the director of pediatric surgical oncology at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute in Boston, who worked on the study.
“They are at higher risks for more aggressive types of colorectal cancers and more opportunities for diagnostic delays,” she said.
Cameron stressed that cases in adolescents and very young adults are “still very, very rare.” But anecdotally, experts say they are seeing rates begin to tick up.
Worldwide, rates of colorectal cancer are rising among people in their 20s and 30s. A person born in the 1990s is four times more likely to be diagnosed with colorectal cancer before age 50 than people born in the 1960s were.
Previous research has focused on colorectal cancer in adults under 50 . Cameron and her team went younger, focusing on people under 21.
The team identified 84 adolescents, with a median age of 16, in the United States who’d been diagnosed with colorectal cancer from 2012 through 2023. (Henderson was not a part of the study and Cameron was not her doctor.) The research will be presented at the American Academy of Pediatrics’ national conference in San Diego on Saturday. It has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Most of the young people in the study, 80%, weren’t diagnosed until their cancer had reached Stage 3 or Stage 4, which means the cancer has spread. That tracks with Henderson’s diagnosis: By the time her cancer was found, it had spread to her ovaries.
Once a cancer has spread, it’s much more difficult to treat — in the study, about 37% of the patients’ cancer returned and 45% of the patients died.
Diagnosing colorectal cancer in adolescents can be challenging. They’re decades away from colonoscopies to screen for the disease, and, according to Cameron, “the symptoms they are presenting with are vague.”
In the study, about 74% of people reported back or abdominal pain , and about 45% reported changes in bowel habits. A similar portion of people reported unexplained weight loss and about 32% had rectal bleeding.
“There are a lot more common things that cause those symptoms,” said Dr. Tara Henderson, chair of the department of pediatrics at the Yale School of Medicine, who was not involved in the research. (Tara and Jo Henderson are not related.)
Dr. Christopher Lieu, co-director of gastrointestinal medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, Colorado, said that not every child or teenager who loses weight or has abdominal pain should get a colonoscopy, “but taking symptoms seriously is important.”
If a doctor has ruled out more common issues such as irritable bowel syndrome and things aren’t improving in the short term, doctors should consider ruling out colorectal cancer, said Lieu, who wasn’t involved with the research.
“If it is colorectal cancer, the more we can catch these cases at early stages of disease, the better outcomes will be,” he said.
And then there’s “the million-dollar question,” as Cameron calls it: What’s causing the rise in colorectal cancer in young people?
She suspects that it likely has to do with DNA changes brought on by environmental exposures during childhood.
Dr. Kimmie Ng, the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, said that the rise in ultraprocessed food could be playing a role. Ng, who is Jo Henderson’s oncologist, noted that her previous research found that women who ate more ultraprocessed foods had a higher risk of colon polyps that can be precursors to cancer. Studies looking at whether microplastics could play a role are ongoing, she said.
A common risk factor for colorectal cancer is having a first- or second-degree relative — a parent, sibling, grandparent, aunt or uncle — who’d had the disease. But that was only the case for 20% of the people in the study.
However, “despite there being no family history, they may still have a genetic predisposition,” said Tara Henderson.
About half of the patients in the study underwent genetic testing, which revealed a handful of genetic mutations that can raise the risk of cancer. These mutations aren’t necessarily inherited; instead they can be caused by certain exposures, or simply by chance.
“It really does suggest that some of the exposures that are occurring early in life are playing a role in early-onset colorectal cancer,” Lieu said.
After her diagnosis, Jo Henderson launched into treatment. In December, she had a portion of her colon removed, as well as both of her ovaries, before undergoing five months of chemotherapy. She’s on hormone replacement medicine and will need annual colonoscopies moving forward.
A colonoscopy in August showed no signs of cancer. It was just four days before she was due to move away to college. She’s now a freshman in the Powers College of Business at Clemson University.
Kaitlin Sullivan is a contributor for NBCNews.com who has worked with NBC News Investigations. She reports on health, science and the environment and is a graduate of the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at City University of New York.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: Back in the Saddle: True Waller’s journey from spinal surgery to world champion
articles.title_zh: Back in the Saddle: True Waller’s journey from spinal surgery to world champion
articles.content_orig:
Cleveland junior True Waller didn't let a back injury slow her down from carrying on her family's legacy and giving back to help others.
It's easy to pull into Blythewood Farms and think, this is all just horse play. But what lies beneath the mane is a family legacy that dates back to 1942.
"My great grandmother Bess Neil made this created this farm, and it's been passed down since to my grandma, and my mom and my sister and I are continuing to ride and continuing to kind of keep that dream going," Cleveland High School junior, and junior exhibition horse show world champion, True Waller said.
"It means it means a lot. Yeah, get a little emotional about it, really, but this is you know a pretty amazing place, and it's meant a lot to a lot of people for a lot of years," True’s mother, Key Waller, added.
Given the family tradition, it may be surprising that True Waller's passion was volleyball. Until a back injury changed everything.
"I had three herniated discs in my spine, so I had a spinal discectomy. So, it was spinal surgery, and it was July. I had my surgery July 2025," True said.
"Of course, that was really difficult because you know it's spinal surgery on a 14-year-old," Key said.
Due to her injury, True can't ride on horseback. But like her great grandmother before her, she rides saddle seat. And like her mother and sister, True is now a world champion. What some would call a setback; the Waller family calls fate.
"It's really nice knowing that I could do it myself, and like, obviously, like being in this family is very honoring just because of our ancestry. But being able to honor it as well is very awesome."
Rehabbing from spinal surgery at 14 years old to becoming a world champion, no one said growing up would be easy. But now, True is looking to make things easier for other young athletes rehabbing from injuries through her non-profit Revive and Thrive.
"I just think that giving an opportunity to athletes like that is something that I want to do because I was able to have that opportunity. But not everybody does, and it was something that was super important to me because I experienced it," True said.
Life always has a way of bucking you off course. But it's all about saddling back up towards your true purpose.
"Just being able to share my story, I think, is important because, like, yes, I got out of it, but it wasn't easy, and like I did go through that as well,” True said.
“I think sharing that is important to other athletes. Like they're not alone."

articles.title_orig: Former world champion boxers to face off in bare-knuckle fight
articles.title_zh: Former world champion boxers to face off in bare-knuckle fight
articles.content_orig:
Two former world champion boxers plan to fight without something that once defined them – boxing gloves.
Victor Ortiz and Paulie Malignaggi will face off in a bare-knuckle fight Dec. 5 when they headline the BKB Bare Knuckle Boxing event in Los Angeles, BKB confirmed to USA TODAY Sports.
It will be a super welterweight fight scheduled for five rounds at the Opheum Theater.
"To make boxing fans show up for bare knuckle, you gotta put two big-name boxers in the mix," Malignaggi told USA TODAY Sports. "And I think right now, this is one of the biggest fights you can make in the whole sport of bare knuckle."
Malignaggi, 45, is almost two decades removed from winning the IBF world super lightweight championship. Ortiz, 39, won the WBC world welterweight title in 2011.
But both have waded into world of bare-knuckle boxing.
Ortiz signed with BKB in March and made his debut in July, when he knocked down Dominic Salcido and won a five-round bout by unanimous decision. Ortiz emerged from the fight grinning even though his left eye was swollen shut.
"I don't think that these punches hurt more than life in itself," Ortiz told USA TODAY Sports.
Malignaggi made his debut in 2025, when he suffered broken ribs, facial cuts that required stitches and bloodied hands on his way to a split-decision victory over Tyler Goodjohn.
BKB's triangular ring, a tight-quartered space known as the Trigon, leaves little room for fighters to evade action, according to Malignaggi.
"People remember my (boxing) style," Malignaggi said. "It was a very defensive-mind style, But in this sport, especially in the Trigon, there's not going to be a lot of holding … Two boxers are going to go with what they know how to do, and that's swing and throw punches and then look for meaningful striking shots, slashing each other up."
Tyson Fury, the former two-time world heavyweight champion, has expressed interest in in fighting bare-knuckle. Of course that's clearly on hold why he prepares for his highly anticipated bout with Anthony Joshua Dec. 11 .
But David Tetreault, CEO of of BKB, said he's talked to Fury about the possibility of a bareknuckle fight. Tetreault said he's also talked about the possibility with Andy Ruiz, the former heavyweight world champion who has provided commentary during BKB broadcasts.
"Those conversations are active," Tetreault told USA TODAY Sports. "It all comes down to the way that we could create a mega event.
"It could be with other heavyweights that are out there. But if we can construct the proper mega event, we have the funding and the way to make that come together."
In 2015, Tetreault joined Oscar La Hoya's Golden Boy Promotions as an executive. He said for years prior to that, there was a talk about a matchup between Ortiz and Malignaggi. It'll finally set to happen, albeit it in a triangular ring and without gloves.
"And with the two of them having the pedigree of both being former world champions, it's a really big deal," Tetreault said.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Former world champion boxers to face off in bare-knuckle fight

articles.title_orig: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.title_zh: World Forest Week: FAO urges greater investment and action for the world's dryland forests
articles.content_orig:
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale
Dryland forests provide vital ecosystems, resources and livelihoods for communities around the world.
Rome – Forests and trees in the world's drylands sustain the livelihoods, food security and cultural identity of more than two billion people, yet they remain insufficiently recognized in global climate, biodiversity and land agendas, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
FAO’s Call to Action on Dryland Forests was launched today during a High-level dialogue on Dryland forests for food, nutrition and resilience held as part of the 10th World Forest Week, running alongside the 28th Session of the FAO Committee on Forestry (COFO) at FAO headquarters in Rome.
The call urges governments, donors and partners to strengthen the sustainable management, restoration and governance of drylands forests; better integrate them into national climate, biodiversity and land priorities; and significantly increase investment in their conservation and sustainable use. It also proposes a new Dryland Forest Support Accelerator as an enabling platform to speed up implementation, mobilize finance, and strengthen country-driven action at scale.
“Dryland forests are central to our lives, and that of future generations,” said FAO Director-General QU Dongyu in a video message. “Yet dryland forests are often underrecognized, under-monitored and under-financed. This must change.”
Drylands - which are characterized by water scarcity - host forests, woodlands and trees outside forests and cover roughly 41 percent of the Earth's land surface. They also account for 27 percent of global forest area.
Drylands produce high-demand wood and non-wood products, buffer people against drought, and provide one of the most accessible safety nets for the world's poorest households – from fuelwood and fodder to wild foods and medicinal plants. They also underpin the resilience of agrifood systems by supporting livestock, protecting soils and water resources, and providing food and income when crops fail.
But around 25 percent of dryland forest ecosystems are already degraded, driven largely by land-use change including agricultural expansion, urbanization and unsustainable resource extraction. Climate change is compounding these pressures, with longer droughts intensifying water stress and increasing fire risk. These impacts fall heavily on smallholders, Indigenous Peoples, pastoralists and local communities, as well as women and youth.
Dryland Forest Support Accelerator
The Call to Action emphasizes that proven solutions for reviving drylands already exist, and the priority is to create the conditions to implement them at scale.
At the centre of the call is the Dryland Forest Support Accelerator – an FAO-anchored, country-driven platform to help move action beyond fragmented projects. It would support countries in integrating dryland forests into national planning processes – including nationally determined contributions and land degradation neutrality targets – accessing long-term finance, strengthening monitoring, and improving coordination across sectors.
Building on FAO’s experience on drylands, notably through the GEF-7 Dryland Sustainable Landscapes Impact Program and the COFO Working Group on Dryland Forests and Agrosilvopastoral Systems, the Accelerator would organize support around three objectives:  gathering evidence and identifying country needs; supporting the implementation and scaling of proven approaches; and capturing results and lessons to inform future action.
The Call to Action further advises that governments, donors and the Rio Conventions give greater political and financial priority to dryland forests across global environmental processes, including through formal recognition of dryland forests as a priority ecosystem under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD).

articles.title_zh: Moon World Resorts advances plans for moon-shaped experiential resorts
articles.content_orig:
Giant spherical destinations are planned across the world
The Moon World Resorts project is now progressing from concept into the design and engineering stages
Moon World Resorts' vision for moon-shaped experiential destinations is moving forwards, with the project now progressing from concept into the design and engineering stages.
The company has selected consulting engineering firm Entuitive to support the development of the spherical resorts from design through construction.
The proposed Moon sites are described as the world's most innovative experiential destinations, and are planned for North and South America, Europe, the Middle East, Asia, Oceania and Africa.
They will integrate hospitality, entertainment, wellness, education, technology, attractions, space training, Earth-based space tourism and more.
Moon World Resorts' vision for moon-shaped experiential destinations is moving forwards Moon
"Entuitive is thrilled to be working with Moon World Resorts on this groundbreaking development that will redefine hospitality industry standards," said Barry Charnish , founding principal at Entuitive.
"It's been a great honour to witness the development of the vision of Moon and now quite exciting to kick off this global initiative.
"Moon's signature true sphere and the surrounding 556-acre masterplan are the types of projects that fuel an engineer’s desire to keep designing and creating to push the limits of the built environment."
Sandra G. Matthews , co-founder and president of Moon World Resorts , said: "Barry has supported Moon World Resorts, the vision behind Moon, since inception."
"Entuitive delivers the structural discipline and building envelope expertise a project of Moon's scale and ambition demands," she added.
"Barry's decades of tall building leadership provides absolute confidence in the entire engineering foundation footprint."
In addition, Moon World Resorts has appointed Toronto-based firm BDP Quadrangle as lead architects across its planned Moon resorts.
"A project of this scale cannot be the product of a single discipline working in isolation; it requires architects, engineers, and specialists working as equals toward a shared vision," said Matthews.
