articles.title_orig: Campaign-style Trump ads use money meant for border security, memorials
articles.title_zh: Campaign-style Trump ads use money meant for border security, memorials
articles.content_orig:
A GOP senator blocked a resolution on Tuesday that criticized the Trump administration’s recent taxpayer-funded ads promoting President Donald Trump.
Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming objected to the Democrat-led measure, which stated that taxpayer funds should not have been used for the controversial ads.
The measure, from Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, slammed the administration for using government funds for the White House’s recent advertisements. “It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language ‘paid for by the U.S. Government,’ should not be paid for by the United States government,” it read.
Senators on both sides of the aisle have criticized the president for using taxpayer dollars for the ads. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday, “It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” and retiring GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas added, “no” it’s not appropriate. “It’s not even a close question,” he said.
On the Senate floor on Tuesday, as she introduced her resolution, Hassan said, “The American people want their tax dollars to go towards helping them and keeping them safe, not propaganda campaigns for a president. He’s welcome to run whatever ads he wants with his own riches, but with taxpayer dollars, money that people have worked hard to earn, he needs to follow the law.”
Lummis echoed the White House’s own argument that the ads are comparable to public service announcements released during previous administrations, and are not campaign ads.
“Presidents of both parties have used public service announcements to speak directly to the American people for decades,” the Wyoming Republican said. “The message at the heart of these PSAs is a simple one: American values are worth defending against the failed ideologies of communism and socialism. If that is what has the senator from New Hampshire concerned, I’d suggest the concern says more about her side of the aisle than it does about the PSA.”
One recently released taxpayer-funded television ad features imagery of Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad .
Hassan attempted to pass the resolution criticizing the use of taxpayer funding for the ads via a fast-track process known as a unanimous consent request. Any single senator can object to such a request.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday defended the ads, arguing they are not political because he is not on the ballot.
“Well, I’m not running for office, first of all, and so the ads are given by me, but I’m not running for office, and I don’t talk about anybody,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
The president described the spots as patriotic messaging rather than campaign material. “But when I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The Way the World Ends: Braves 6, Phillies 2
articles.title_zh: The Way the World Ends: Braves 6, Phillies 2
articles.content_orig:
Surely some revelation is at hand.
“Not with a bang, but with a whimper.” So wrote T.S. Eliot. He was many things, but he was not a baseball fan: if he had been, he would’ve known that the world, or at least a season, can end with both. The Phillies and their fans know this well: their 2026 ended with the bangs of Braves home runs, and the whimpers of their own offense.
It began quietly for the Phillies. Kyle Schwarber singled to left against Braves opener Ray Kerr, but Bryce Harper went down whiffing on a cutter, and Bohm grounded out.
Aaron Nola went down 3-0 on Ronald Acuña Jr. , eventually walking him, then went down 3-0 again against Matt Olson, walking him too. His pitches could not find the strike zone. What happened next has happened many times this season, and happened again tonight: Nola gave up a gopher ball. Michael Harris saw a pitch that was quite low, delivered a perfect swing, knocked it into right field, and the Phillies were down 3-0. Nola’s second inning saw him put the first two Braves down, though they made good contact. Dominic Smith did not, though he did enough: he dribbled one straight back, just far enough to get on base. Nola was pulled, and replaced with Tim Mayza, who quickly wrapped up the inning.
The Phillies offense couldn’t do damage against Kerr, and so the deficit remained at three as Zack Wheeler came out for the bottom third. He immediately encountered trouble, as Acuña smacked a line drive that bounced off of Trea Turner for a leadoff single. But he was sent back to the dugout on a fielder’s choice, and Wheeler navigated the rest of the inning without incident.
Kerr returned for the fourth, the Phillies still unable to solve him, and the Phillies got their second baserunner of the night on via a Kyle Schwarber walk. Bryce Harper hit a hard line drive, which Mauricio Dubon grabbed on a dive, tossing to second to put Schwarber out. Kerr was replaced with Grant Holmes, who bobbled a grounder from Alec Bohm but got the out anyway, and the Phillies left their half of the fourth still scoreless. Their season was teetering on the brink, and soon it fell over: Wheeler walked Austin Riley, then gave up a homer to Ozzie Albies. Braves fans, full of passionate intensity, performed their typical pantomime.
With the mood thoroughly nauseous, the Phillies finally got some breaks: Bryan De La Cruz singled to open the fifth, and a wild pitch advanced him to second. Brandon Marsh replaced Edmundo Sosa as a pinch hitter and negotiated his way to ball four. But the glimmer of hope vanished, snuffed out by a twin killing. The Phillies put another baserunner aboard in the sixth (Schwarber, single to right), chasing Holmes, who was replaced by Robert Suarez. Harper doubled to right, and Schwarber scored on a groundout from Bohm. The Phillies would not go into the night scoreless.
Wheeler continued into the sixth, walking two with two outs, but working his way to the last out without further damage incurred. The offense was punchless in the seventh, and Jonathan Bowlan was asked to keep Atlanta’s the same. He could not: Matt Olson homered.
Derek Hill, pinch-hitting for Justin Crawford, tripled in the eighth as a ball slipped past a leaping Acuña Jr; he scored on a sacrifice fly from Turner. Chris Sale was brought in to face Harper, who flailed to a strikeout. Jhoan Duran took the eighth, preventing the deficit from getting worse. Sale returned for the final frame.
Alec Bohm, in possibly his last at-bat as a Phillie, singled to center. Bryson Stott foul popped out, De La Cruz struck out, Otto Kemp did the same, and all was silence.

articles.title_orig: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.title_zh: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.content_orig:
by Jackie Kent, KOMO News Reporter
SEATTLE — Boeing has avoided an engineering strike after more than 17,000 engineers and technical workers on Thursday approved a four-year contract offer promising wage increases and other perks.
The Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace wrapped up its electronic voting at noon.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Boeing releases final contract offer to union engineers, technical workers
The bargaining team had recommended members accept the offer as it guarantees a 34% pay boost over four years, including a nearly immediate 10% increase in October. The deal also enhances health care and retirement benefits and adds two vacation days, a new floating holiday, and three bereavement days.
Alex Phillips is a software security engineer for Boeing in Seattle, and he's been fighting for a big pay bump.
"To improve members’ lives and help Boeing do better," Phillips explained. "There’s a lot of things in this contract that I think are stepping stones for making improvements."
Kevin Boyd works out of the Auburn facility as a cutting tool designer, and said it was critical for this contract to increase base salaries.
"I hope this is a foundation we can continue to build a relationship with Boeing," Boyd added.
The agreement means the aerospace company has narrowly avoided a shutdown of engineering development and regulatory compliance at a time when Boeing is under pressure to improve build quality and clear its aircraft backlog.
"The stakes were really high. Certification of the new Boeing 777 and the [Boeing 737] MAX 10 kind of hung in the balance. Those programs surely would’ve been delayed if the engineers and technicians had gone on strike," Leeham News and Analysis Editor Howard Hardee explained. The trade publication and consulting firm tracks Boeing's production struggles, regulatory hurdles and labor relations.
The machinists went on strike for nearly two months in 2024, which hurt the company's bottom line, brought commercial activity across the Puget Sound area to a standstill and hurt efforts to ramp up production rates for the 737 MAX program. Hardee said that's what Boeing wanted to avoid happening again in this round of negotiations.
"Generally speaking, [Boeing has] had  series of wins. They got the MAX 7 certified," Hardee stated. "They have had a setback on certification of the MAX 10, but getting this negotiation process behind them I think is a really positive development for Boeing, and for people watching the industry it can only be a good sign of their continued recovery."
The company has said these final amounts are $11,000 more for professional employees and $8,000 more for technical workers than under its initial offer, which the union rejected in August.
Following the vote to approve the contract offers, Boeing issued this statement:
“We’re pleased with the outcome of the vote. We look forward to working with our team to support our company’s continued recovery and meeting our customer commitments now and into the future.” – Ben Nimmergut, vice president and functional chief engineer for Production Engineering

articles.title_orig: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.title_zh: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.content_orig:
Nike on Thursday posted a mixed fiscal first quarter and announced a restructuring plan that will lead to layoffs starting next year.
The company also offered a full-year outlook, saying it expects revenues to decline by a high-single digit percentage in fiscal 2027. Nike also said it expects adjusted earnings per share to be in a range of $1.15 to $1.35.
Shares of Nike fell roughly 3% in extended trading Thursday.
Here's what the company reported for the period compared to what analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Nike reported net income of $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the year prior.
Revenue fell 4% to $11.21 billion. The retailer said Nike brand revenues took a hit largely due to sustained declines in the China business. Revenue in the market dropped 26%. CEO Elliott Hill said on a call with analysts that the company is "moving with urgency" to improve its business in the region.
Its North America revenue came in at $5.13 billion, just above estimates of $5.11 billion, according to StreetAccount. Nike also reported gross margin of 42.8% compared to estimates of 42.4%.
"Despite that progress, our Nike performance business is not yet large enough to offset the pressure we're seeing in Nike Sportswear, Jordan Brand, and Greater China," Hill told analysts. "We're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses, but realizing the full benefit of those efforts will take time."
Nike's sportswear segment, which Hill said accounted for just under half of the quarter's revenue, fell by a low-double digit percentage.
" Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic," he said on the call. "Yes, the consumer is cautious, but as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear."
The sneaker giant also announced a restructuring plan to "position Nike for long-term growth." The strategy is expected to result in layoffs beginning in 2027, though the company did not provide any further details on how many jobs it would cut.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill wrote in a letter to the company.
The cuts are the third round of layoffs Nike has announced this year.
The company said it plans to focus on its supply chain modernization, organizing into three geographies, building a new campus in India and changing its work and workforce. Those geographic regions will be the Americas; the Asia Pacific and Greater China; and Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The strategy, which Nike has dubbed Pace, is expected to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. It'll also result in a 15-cent restructuring expense to fiscal 2027 earnings per share, the company added.
"We expect Pace to streamline decision making, so we can capture demand faster and improve productivity, while also creating greater capacity to invest in what has always set Nike apart: serving athletes, creating industry-leading innovation and building the world's strongest sports brands," Hill said on the conference call.
The retailer has been in the midst of a turnaround plan, focused on improving separate parts of its business at different rates based on priority. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions and higher inflation lead to slower spending.
Shares of Nike have plummeted more than 40% this year.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Energy Department employee on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Energy Department employee on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Fox News correspondent Steve Harrigan reports on Iran-backed Houthi rebel gains in the strategic Red Sea region. Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs joins to discuss President Trump urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
A U.S. Department of Energy worker from Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and charged with attempting to provide "material support" to the Iran-backed Houthis, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, is accused of attempting to use his electrical engineering knowledge and background to support the terrorist group in improving its mobile communications infrastructure, secure components for drones as well as chemicals for homemade explosives.
"As alleged, a U.S. government employee traveled overseas and used his specialized expertise in an attempt to aid the Houthis, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization backed by Iran," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said in a statement.
"Additionally, Ellaboudy acquired materials for the construction of explosive material and drones capable of delivering these explosives. These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination."
IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR
A Houthi follower during a pro-Iran demonstration in Sanaa, Yemen, April 6, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)
Federal authorities took Ellaboudy into custody after an investigation by the FBI’s Inland Northwest Joint Terrorism Task Force .
According to court records, Ellaboudy first attracted the FBI’s attention after he allegedly bought precursor chemicals, or starting ingredients, and components often used in homemade explosives, as well as parts to make drones .
The DOJ said that, in 2024, Ellaboudy took sick leave from his Department of Energy job and said he had been exposed to highly concentrated nitric acid, a key chemical compound used in explosive manufacturing .
FBI OFFERS $200K REWARD FOR FORMER AIR FORCE INTELLIGENCE AGENT ACCUSED OF SPYING FOR IRAN
Houthi supporters demonstrate in solidarity with Iran during a two-week ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran in Sanaa, Yemen, April 10, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)
In 2025, prosecutors allege, Ellaboudy used an official passport from his previous role with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to travel from Washington state to Oman.
He then crossed into Yemen. After returning to the U.S., Ellaboudy allegedly told border officers his trip was authorized government business.
Investigators also said Ellaboudy advised an undercover FBI confidential human source posing as a representative of a Houthi colonel.
For the Houthis, Ellaboudy allegedly tested solar generators, modified power systems, created circuit schematics and provided support to the group’s communications, the statement said.
NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS
The U.S. Department of Energy headquarters June 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

articles.title_orig: Lancaster County Coroner urges vaccination after third measles-associated death
articles.title_zh: Lancaster County Coroner urges vaccination after third measles-associated death
articles.content_orig:
The Lancaster County coroner is calling for vaccinations after the Department of Health reported a third measles-associated death, raising concerns about rising cases during colder months.
The Lancaster County coroner is calling for vaccinations after the Department of Health reported a third measles-associated death, raising concerns about rising cases during colder months.
Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni is urging residents to get vaccinated as the state’s Department of Health reports a third measles-associated death, citing concerns about increased exposure to infectious diseases during the colder season.
"I would guess the number of total cases will increase," Diamantoni said. "As it gets cold, more people will be inside and in close proximity to each other, and measles is highly infectious. Certainly, if an individual has measles and they're in a closed space, a room, you know, they can easily spread that infection to other individuals within that space."
The Department of Health informed the coroner about the third measles-associated death but did not provide further details.
"I wanted to know whether that death was actually caused by measles or somebody died from something else and may have had measles, but they were not willing to share any of that information with me," he said.
The coroner also questioned the Department of Health’s use of the term "measles-associated."
"That's not a term that we use. What we look at is what the cause of death is and the manner of death is," the coroner said.
The Department of Health stated it is not required to report measles-associated deaths to the coroner.
Both the Department of Health and the coroner emphasized the importance of vaccination.
"For a single dose of the vaccine, just one dose, there's 93% protection. If people have both doses of the vaccine, the protection goes up to 97%," the Department of Health said.
The coroner added, "If people have both vaccines, they're fully vaccinated against measles and the other respiratory illnesses that are oftentimes rampant during the winter."

articles.title_zh: US deploys thousands more troops, Marines to Middle East as oil prices surge
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of September, ending a 23-year presence.
The U.S. military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday.
The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria .
"Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
Soldiers from the U.S.-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the U.S.-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (The Associated Press)
"Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland," Cooper said.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the departure the formal conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and said it marked a transition "from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Pentagon said the U.S. will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi forces even after the withdrawal, while Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga, take the lead in keeping ISIS remnants suppressed.
Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations , according to CENTCOM.
U.S. and coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30. The withdrawal followed an agreement reached between Washington and Baghdad under the Biden administration in 2024 and carried forward under the Trump administration.
Admiral Charles Bradford "Brad" Cooper II, commander of U.S. Central Command, speaks during a joint press conference at CENTCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, on March 5, 2026. (Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images)
Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE
The U.S. has roughly 4,000 troops stationed in Jordan, where American forces will continue monitoring the ISIS threat. Muwaffaq Salti Air Base hosts U.S. combat aircraft and has itself become a target during the conflict with Iran. Three U.S. service members were killed in an Iranian attack on the base in July.
"As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said.
"Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added.
The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.
With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014. (REUTERS/Mohammed Ameen)
For the last several years, roughly 2,500 U.S. troops have been stationed in Iraq. The majority departed last year, leaving hundreds of troops in the northern Kurdish region until the final withdrawal.
The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming.
IRANIAN PRESIDENT BLAMES US FOR MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT WHILE DENYING NUCLEAR AMBITIONS, OFFERS TO DILUTE URANIUM
The Pentagon explicitly identified those militias as one of the security challenges Baghdad will now be expected to confront.
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," Parnell said.
The withdrawal also reduces the number of U.S. military targets inside Iraq after American forces there faced repeated attacks by Iran-aligned groups following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. During this year's war with Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks were killed in Iraq, according to Fox News reporting.
The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats.
Kurdish officials say their region has faced more than 1,000 Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks since the war with Iran began Feb. 28, adding to concerns over the removal of U.S. forces and air-defense capabilities.
Thousands of ISIS fighters also remain in Iraq and Syria despite the collapse of the terror group's organized military threat. The Iraqi government has said its forces will continue operations against ISIS, while the Pentagon said the U.S. remains committed to preventing the group from reconstituting from Iraqi territory.

CENTCOM said U.S. and coalition forces elsewhere in the region will remain prepared to respond if ISIS again poses a threat.
"The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries," Parnell said.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.title_zh: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.title_zh: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.content_orig:
The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January , spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits.
“She was pure love, and she was funny, and she was smart, and she was gorgeous,” Becca Good said at a news conference, becoming emotional as she discussed attending back-to-school night and preparing to celebrate Halloween with their children alone.
“Every single one of these moments for all of her babies and for everyone up here was a monumental moment, and she should be here for all of them. We were all robbed,” she said.
Earlier in the news conference, attorneys for Renee Good’s family announced lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force in her Jan. 7 death.
One lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, emotional distress and negligence.
The second suit names Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot Good, as well as several federal officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
“Every morning she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca Good said.
Renee Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said her death was “completely senseless.”
“We file these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten,” he said.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A representative for Ross could not immediately be identified.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the office will “vigorously defend” the claims in the lawsuits. Bis also shared a statement from President Donald Trump, who said Good’s “actions were pretty tough.”
“When you look at the way that car was pulled away ... there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad,” Trump said.
Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a Jan. 7 encounter with Ross. The killing occurred about a month after the Trump administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge. Agents descended on Minnesota after right-wing influencers drew attention to a state fraud scandal involving Somali nationals.
The operation triggered massive protests and significant pushback from state leaders. It ended in February .
The shooting was captured on cellphone video. It showed Good’s partner, Becca Good , standing outside the SUV calling Ross “big boy” and telling him to remove the covering from his face. Other officers at the scene could be heard telling Good to get out of the car. In the video, Good is seen turning the steering wheel away from Ross and beginning to drive.
Multiple gunshots can be heard in the video before Good’s SUV crashes into a parked car. In a separate video recorded by Ross, a male voice could be heard saying “f-----g b----” moments before the crash.
Trump administration figures, including President Donald Trump and Noem, defended Ross’ actions and claimed Good was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle. Witnesses told NBC News at the time that Ross didn’t appear to be in the direct path of the SUV.
Noem said Ross was treated at a hospital for injuries he sustained in the incident and was released soon after. A DHS official previously told NBC News that Ross sustained internal bleeding but did not elaborate on his injuries.
Attorney Antonio M. Romanucci, who is representing Good’s family, said he hopes the lawsuits “are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers.”
Weeks after Good’s killing, Customs and Border Protection agents shot and killed Alex Pretti , a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, in Minneapolis.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.
The claims, which sent related hashtags trending on social media late last month, centred on three sites in Xunyang where archaeologists last year found evidence of cinnabar mining, processing and transport during the pre-Qin and Qin-Han periods.

articles.title_zh: World premiere of ʻAinakea opens Friday at Historic ʻĪao Theater
articles.content_orig:
Privacy Policy | About Our Ads
Maui OnStage will present the world premiere of ʻAinakea.  PC: courtesy
Maui OnStage will present the world premiere of ʻAinakea , a new play by Maui playwright James Nevius, opening Friday, October 2, at the Historic ʻĪao Theater. Set in West Maui in 1953, the play explores a family, a plantation and an island on the cusp of profound change.
Hawaiʻi is still a territory, the plantation economy is shifting, and the Goodale family—descendants of early missionaries and longtime owners of the sugar plantation ʻAinakea—is running out of money. As family, friends and plantation workers gather to confront the future of the estate, a larger question emerges: Who should be the stewards of the land?
Inspired by Anton Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard , ʻAinakea brings that classic story of a changing social order into a distinctly Maui setting, exploring labor, family, Hawaiian identity, memory and the changing island.
“This is a story about a particular place and a particular moment in Maui’s history, but the questions it raises are much bigger,” said Luana Whitford-Mitchell, Executive Director of Maui OnStage. “What happens when the world we know begins to change? And who gets to decide what happens to the land? We’re excited to bring James Nevius’ work to the stage for its world premiere.”
Directed by Francis Tauʻa, ʻAinakea features a Maui cast and creative team whose work creates a strong sense of time and place.
Scenic Designer Amanda Dellinger’s set takes its inspiration from the Hanakaʻōʻō ahupuaʻa (land division) located in the moku (district) of Kāʻanapali, including a backdrop based on the silhouette of the West Maui mountain range above the former Puʻukoliʻi Village camp. She also honors the memory of two historic Lahaina buildings lost in the wildfires by incorporating three colors from Ameritone-Maui’s Lahaina Restoration Foundation historic color palette.
Costume Designer Sarah Loney Mark combines true vintage and vintage-inspired pieces to evoke 1953 Maui. Vince Pinelli’s evocative lighting and the collaborative atmospheric sound design of Dawn Harper and Sam Castillo further immerse audiences in the world of ʻAinakea .
Audiences will have an opportunity to hear directly from James Nevius during Talk Story with the Playwright , held immediately following the Sunday performances on Oct. 4 and Oct. 11 .
What: ʻAinakea — World Premiere When: Oct. 2–18, 2026 Performances: Fridays at 7:30 p.m.; Saturdays and Sundays at 3 p.m. Were: Historic ʻĪao Theater, 68 N. Market Street, Wailuku Tickets: $10–$45 Tickets and Information: MauiOnStage.com | 808-242-6969
Maui OnStage extends a special mahalo to its 2026 Season Sponsor, Wave of Harmony Foundation in partnership with Marji Knowles and Michael Tibbott .
Maui OnStage is Maui’s community theater company, presenting live theater and educational performing arts experiences at the historic ʻĪao Theater in Wailuku. Founded in 1931, Maui OnStage has been part of Maui’s performing arts community for more than nine decades.

articles.title_orig: Putin says the world is living through a dangerous moment, warns West not to escalate
articles.title_zh: Putin says the world is living through a dangerous moment, warns West not to escalate
articles.content_orig:
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack.
The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.
Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.
Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.
Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.
He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.
"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.
Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.
Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".
Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

articles.title_orig: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.title_zh: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.
UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes
"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."
However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.
Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.
Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.
He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."
Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel , unlike the UAE.
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.
At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title_orig: Massachusetts man accused of cyberstalking campaign against Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: Massachusetts man accused of cyberstalking campaign against Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X , referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: FIFA World Cup Matches Bring $850 Million to Bay Area, Report Says
articles.title_zh: FIFA World Cup Matches Bring $850 Million to Bay Area, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA World Cup generated roughly $850 million in economic impact in the Bay Area, according to a new report released by regional organizers.
The report was unveiled Thursday by the Bay Area Host Committee, a nonprofit formed to bring major sporting events to the region, with a board of directors made up of heads of local professional sports teams, whose venues often host events or play supporting roles.
The estimated figure is based on metrics evaluating spending by visitors, teams and companies on things like hotels, food, transportation and events, and the wages earned by workers in the region related to the World Cup. The report was prepared for the host committee by Boston Consulting Group.
“Hosting FIFA World Cup 2026 elevated our global reputation, strengthened community bonds and will pay dividends for years to come,” Zaileen Janmohamed, the president & CEO of the host committee, said in a statement.
“The world’s attention on our region showcased the Bay Area as a premier destination for major international events, brought neighbors together through watch parties and shared celebration, and will continue to fuel future tourism as visitors who experienced our hospitality choose to return and recommend the Bay to friends and family,” she said.
The report said the lion’s share of the impacts — about $410 million — were seen in Santa Clara County. Levi’s Stadium, in the city of Santa Clara, was designated as the sole venue for all six World Cup matches played in Northern California.
The stadium was stripped of its branding under FIFA rules, and temporarily dubbed San Francisco Bay Area Stadium .
About $240 million of the boost was felt in San Francisco County, and the remaining $200 million was spread among eight other Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Mateo, Santa Cruz, Solano and Sonoma, according to the report.
The matches and supporting events and celebrations supported “approximately 5,100 jobs across the region and drew an estimated 240,000 visitors from outside the Bay Area, underscoring the tournament’s reach across the region’s hospitality, retail and service sectors,” the host committee’s statement said.
The $850 million figure exceeded the committee’s previous projections for economic impact, which the organization pegged at $480 million to $630 million. It attributed the increase to higher-than-anticipated daily visitor spending.
“The world saw what we’ve known all along — the Bay Area is a world-class sports [region] that excels in bringing people together, welcoming fans from around the globe and delivering an extraordinary World Cup experience,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
“This success was a true team effort, and I could not be more excited for the major sports events to come in the Bay Area.”
The combined events of the 2025 NBA All-Star Game at Chase Center in San Francisco, and Super Bowl LX and the World Cup matches at Levi’s Stadium, generated roughly $1.9 billion for the region in total, according to the host committee.
However, the eye-popping totals proffered by organizations like the host committee are frequently called into question by economics experts and academics.
Roger Noll, a professor emeritus of economics at Stanford University, previously characterized the estimates in such reports as “grossly overstated” and said they serve mainly as public relations or advertising to help justify the large logistical lift, interruptions to public life and costs of hosting major events in the region.
The report prepared for the Super Bowl and other similar events often do not account for mitigating factors, such as the “substitution effect” of people who choose not to visit the Bay Area for business or tourism when major events are held here to avoid higher hotel prices and congestion, he said previously.
But for events like the World Cup, with multiple matches with days in between each, Noll said visitors would likely stay for longer and spend money here.
The boost from the World Cup was undeniable in downtown San José, where the San José Earthquakes hosted a watch party for all 104 matches over 39 days at San Pedro Square Market.
Closed streets and massive viewing screens, along with special permission from the city to allow outdoor drinking, drew thousands of people into the area for matches.
Mayor Matt Mahan’s office said the watch parties, activities and entertainment options in downtown brought 1 million cumulative visits to the area.
While most of the celebrations were peaceful, police reported some shootings and stabbings in the area following some of the events, and huge crowds forced organizers to relocate one viewing party to nearby Discovery Meadow to allow for more space. World Cup events were also canceled at Spark Social in San Francisco after a shooting in the Mission Bay neighborhood.
In June, the Bay Area Host Committee launched a Leadership Council and Corporate Membership Program in support of turning the committee into a “permanent, sustainable sports commission that will secure, support and celebrate major sporting events in the region for decades to come.”
The region is set to host the WNBA All-Star Game in 2027 at Chase Center, and the MLB All-Star Game will return to Oracle Park in 2028. Janmohamed said, with the coming events, “We will continue the incredible momentum of the past two years and directly increase positive economic impact for the Bay.”

articles.title_orig: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.title_zh: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.content_orig:
It's been a difficult few years for Nike.
The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.
The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.
Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more of a marathon than a sprint.
However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.
The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.
To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years.
Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.
So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?
Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available.
"The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.
Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products.
"They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."
That jibe was aimed at John Donahoe, the former eBay boss behind Nike's online direct-to-consumer sales pivot, before he made way for Hill.
Donahoe's four years at Nike coincided with the company's share price plunge.
His tenure saw sales initially soar, driven by pandemic restrictions that boosted online shopping, but subsequent cost-of-living pressures curbed customer spending.
As demand weakened overseas in key markets like China, Nike announced cost cuts and redundancies.
Its digital distraction allowed newer footwear firms on top of the trends to snap at its heels. Shop shelf space previously occupied by Nike was replaced by brands such as On and Hoka.
This was a stark warning to a company that prided and built itself on innovation.
Nike was the firm that signed a deal with a rookie called Michael Jordan in the mid-1980s at a time when the company wasn't a major player in basketball and still mostly known for its running trainers.
The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today.
The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.
In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.
While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024 .
"[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."
Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.
However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.
Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".
Was that a parting dig at Nike?
Derdenger suggests Mbappé's move had parallels to Jordan's decision decades earlier to choose Nike over Converse and Adidas due to the opportunity for the athlete to become synonymous with one brand.
"Athletes have egos and those egos want them to be a part of something big and that they're the ones that are helping drive that change, that growth."
Nike boss Hill said the brand has had "some great moments" with Mbappé over two decades.
"We wish him much success as he makes the move," he said during Nike's earnings call, adding that the brand still has a "great stable of athletes".
For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance.
"Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says.
"When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.
Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.
Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn (£8.3bn), which undershot analysts' expectations.
Notably, the company cited "headwinds" in China, where revenue declined by 26%.
Sales of its Jordan brand were also down globally. Hill said the firm had been "oversupplying" the iconic retro shoe and will now reduce the volume and frequency of products under the brand.
Nike said it expected revenues to decline by "high-single digits" in the financial year ahead, adding that it planned to make savings of $2.5bn by 2031, some of which will result in job losses.
Nike's chief financial officer Dave Denton said: "Our results are below both our expectations and our potential, and we are focused on closing this gap."
The company's shares fell by more than 8% in extended trading in New York after the earnings were announced.
Last year the company launched a spin-off campaign to its iconic "Just Do It" slogan aimed at younger generations with the line "Why Do It?"
Young people, and future sporting stars, may ask themselves: Why Nike?
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

articles.title_orig: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.title_zh: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell on Thursday, giving back some of the recent gains that propelled longer-dated rates to levels not seen in decades.
The 10-year Treasury yield breached a level last seen in April 2002, before easing 5 basis points to 5.243%. The 10-year influences rates on mortgage and auto loans and credit card debt. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also hit its highest in 24 years before dropping more than 2 basis points to 5.613%.
Yields and prices move inversely. One basis point equals 0.01%.
Jeff Kilburg, CEO of KKM Financial, said he sees the 10-year yield pulling back to around 4.5%-4.75% if the U.S. and Iran can reach a deal to end the war. "If we're going to continue to stay in Iran, then that's going to be problematic for the 10-year yield."
Government borrowing costs around the world continued their relentless march upward on Thursday, continuing a monthslong trend as investors voted with their feet over a lack of political will to tackle fiscal deficits, while inflation remains stubbornly above target and leading central banks move to push interest rates higher.
Major economies face "persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses — challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns," the Institute of International Finance said last week .
Japan's 10-year yield hit its highest level since the mid-1990s. Japan's debt has come under pressure from a weaker yen and rate hikes by the Bank of Japan .
The yield on the German 10-year bund, the benchmark for the euro area, topped 3.6%, the highest since 2008, before easing back. Elsewhere in Europe, the French 10-year surged 8 basis points to 4.925%, Italy's 10-year was up 10 basis points to 4.706%, while the U.K.'s 10-year yield increased 5 basis points to 5.483%.
"It's worth noting, but people get pretty worked up about those sorts of spreads regularly, so I don't think it's a crisis point necessarily, as far as Germany versus France or Italy," said Michael Schumacher, former managing director at Wells Fargo. "If you look at some countries that have very poor structural dynamics, like the UK, and I'd be concerned about that. People don't typically trade gilts versus bunds as much, but just as a barometer of, say, market concern, I think that's one to watch."
Bonds had been moving in lockstep with oil prices , which have been turbulent as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran obstructed crude exports from the Middle East. Crude oil prices were higher on Thursday , with international benchmark Brent crude futures back above $100 a barrel.
"We could see [bond] buyers come in effectively to take advantage of those yields, which would have the effect of causing them to go down, but also one of the things that has kept the volatility in those yields in the long end of the curve has been what's going on with oil, what's going on with inflation," Nomi Prins, founder of Prinsights Global, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
But sovereign wealth funds and central banks, among the main long-term holders of Treasury debt, are unlikely to go along, Prins said.
"We could see movement ... in Treasury yields going down if oil prices go down significantly, if there's a resolution" in the Middle East, Prins added.
— With additional reporting from CNBC's Jeff Cox

articles.title_orig: Chicago aldermen question World Business Chicago ads featuring Mayor Johnson
articles.title_zh: Chicago aldermen question World Business Chicago ads featuring Mayor Johnson
articles.content_orig:
Promoting Chicago or promoting the mayor? Aldermen held a hearing on Thursday on World Business Chicago ads, featuring Mayor Johnson. Though, critics say the videos look like campaign commercials.
CHICAGO - Chicago aldermen questioned whether promotional videos produced by World Business Chicago featuring Mayor Brandon Johnson amount to city marketing or political advertising during a hearing Thursday.
Representatives from World Business Chicago did not attend the hearing. Critics argued the videos resemble campaign commercials, while the organization said Johnson is an appropriate spokesperson for the city and that no public funds were used to produce the ads.
World Business Chicago is public and privately financed, so some of your tax dollars do go toward it.
"World Business Chicago is supposed to sell Chicago to the world," said Ald. Samantha Nugent of the 39th Ward. "City and state funding, taxpayer dollars go towards World Business Chicago and taxpayer dollars should not be spent on political advertising, and this appears to be a political advertisement, and that is why we wanted to bring World Business to Chicago to come in for a conversation.
World Business Chicago receives much of its funding from city and state grants. They say touting the economy and billions in investment is core to their mission.
The Source: The information in this report came from statements made during a Chicago City Council hearing, comments from World Business Chicago and Ald. Samantha Nugent, and publicly available information about the organization's funding and mission.
