A year ago today, when Jane Goodall died in Los Angeles, the world lost an icon . I lost one of my oldest, closest friends. Thinking both about that moment and how we should mark this one, I hear her voice urging us to look forward, as fervently as she always did—to the future she spent years preparing others to build, and, above all, to the youth she inspired to follow her.
Years ago, as Jane and I shared a quiet dinner alone in New York during one of her tours, she drolly recounted an incident from her lecture the previous evening. She had filled a very large old theater with people keen to hear her share her history and hopes. After her talk, two long lines of eager questioners filled the aisles. A young girl gushed, “Oh, Dr. Goodall, you’re so amazing! You’ve done so much! What is your next big project?”
Jane’s response was clear, quick, and simple: “My next big project? Death!”
The whole house gasped. Silence followed. Gently, Jane continued: “Let’s be clear. I’m over 80. I travel over 300 days a year. Of course, there’s so much that I still want to do, but no one lives forever. At some point, death becomes the next step. And, as someone who has always looked forward to the next adventure, I’m actually curious about it.”
When, the following night, I joined Jane for dinner at her hotel in Manhattan, bringing vegetarian curries and a bottle of scotch, a combination we both adored, and she described this exchange, I nearly choked on my drink at her unexpected punchline, sputtering, “You really said that?”
She nodded mischievously. But, beneath her smile, I sensed something else. I saw her beginning to prepare the world for a time when she would no longer be here to carry on her work. She was shaping her legacy, focusing forward.
That effort could be traced to her very beginning—and ours. In 1957, my mother, Helen Illick, was appointed Assistant Director for Systematic Biology at the National Science Foundation (NSF) at only 31 years old. Vetting grant applications, she discovered one that captivated her completely: it would support another young woman, one researching chimpanzees in Africa. My mother championed it, and the NSF awarded a generous grant that helped fund Jane’s first field work. The legend, the legacy, and the role of youth in both began right there.
Jane always loved that our mothers, who had shaped our lives most, had been connected from the start, when the funding that my mother helped secure allowed Jane’s mother to join her daughter in her first months in the field. But later, my own work, which took me into conflict zones in Africa, bound me to Jane in even deeper and more direct ways.
Rwanda, during its 1994 genocide , was the most harrowing mission I ever went on for the United Nations. Shattered by what I saw there, I reached out to Jane the moment I returned. We spoke quietly together of the horrors I had witnessed. Then I asked her, “How did you cope when you saw the chimps go to war, when they killed each other right in front of you?” Her eyes filled with a sorrow that mirrored my own.
“I was horrified, Henry—absolutely horrified. But, after the fighting ended, I saw them forgive. They rebuilt their communities and their lives. In many ways, they’re better at forgiveness than we are. I’ve always hoped that we might learn that from them, one day.” We both felt how far away “one day” was in that moment, but that ember of hope still anchored us.
I, however, was not the only troubled youth then turning to Jane. As the Cold War receded and the world briefly brimmed with an optimism that Jane captured and conveyed beautifully, young people—with no direct memory of the World Wars or Cold War—sometimes reflected something different back to her. Some would seek her out privately after she spoke and admit, “I don’t see your reason for hope. I don’t understand it. And I don’t share it.” Gauging the world from a very different starting point, they reached conclusions about its future that history has since often proven prescient.
Jane heard them. Their concerns increasingly shaped her voice, her vision, and her work. In 1991, at Gombe, her research station in Tanzania, she met with 12 teenagers. Their conversation led to the founding of Roots and Shoots , the youth program of her institute, which now has active groups in 75 countries.
When Jane became a United Nations Messenger of Peace , one of these groups proposed building and flying a giant kite in the form of a dove to celebrate both her appointment and the International Day of Peace. When Jane and I joined them, we watched them assemble it. The two tallest teens carried the dove’s papier-mâché head; others unfurled old white bedsheets for its wings, body, and tail. Then the wind caught their creation, and the dove rose into the air. Looking at their faces, we saw how beautifully their hopes rose with it. Then Jane’s hand landed lightly on my arm. As I turned to meet her gaze, I was amazed: her face—always beautiful—was absolutely luminous. She was profoundly, radiantly happy. Then I understood: these youth were helping her keep her own hope aloft as well.
What made that moment so powerful for us was the healing it brought to the grief we were then carrying: Jane and I had both just lost our mothers, the pillars of our lives, mere months apart. Jane often tried to soften that blow by saying, “They’re on a cloud together somewhere, Henry; they’re floating along happily on a cloud, watching over us.” More rarely, and softly, she would add that “one day, we will be there with them.” As others close to us died, Jane would wish them to that cloud as well. When a close friend teased us about “creating an entire cloud contingent,” we happily embraced the term. It became our shared secret, invoked in need and toasted in triumph. And, of course, it became our ultimate destination.
Two years before she died, Jane spoke at Kings Theater in Brooklyn, after returning to touring following her pandemic hiatus. When she reached the lectern, she paused, sensing something. Then, at nearly 90 years old, she suddenly ran a full lap around the empty stage, with the glee of a girl. As her shawl billowed behind her, she seemed almost aflight. By the time she circled back, the entire audience was on its feet cheering. There was no talk of death that night; the moment begged for something completely different, and she sensed it and responded immediately.
Just 10 days before her death, Jane was briefly in Manhattan on what neither of us knew would be her final visit. Sharing curries and scotch at her hotel, we spoke quietly of people we cared about, hopes we were nurturing, and plans we were still making. We toasted the cloud contingent.
Then, on the morning of October first, hundreds of schoolchildren gathered in Pasadena, Calif. to hear Jane speak. Students from communities that had suffered brutal wildfires had founded TREEAMS (Trees + Dreams). Together, they had committed to planting 5,000 trees to help their community recover, and Jane had told me over dinner how much she looked forward to planting the first of these with them.
Unexpectedly, Jane participated in their event differently than planned. She joined them from the cloud, with the rest of the contingent, after the most transformative flight of all. Moments before she was to speak, someone stepped to the lectern to announce her passing. Shock swept through the room, just as it had when she spoke of death years before. Some gasped. Some w

People with low vision can use Guided Vision to have Gemini describe what’s nearby and ask follow-up questions.
Guided Vision is launching in Gemini Live on compatible Android devices today to use AI to give real-time audio descriptions of anything you point your phone’s camera at. By sharing your camera in Gemini Live, you can have Google’s AI help with things like reading small text, describing your surroundings, finding or identifying objects around you, and describing details on specific objects.
Like the VoiceOver Live Recognition feature Apple has added to the iPhone and Vision Pro , it’s designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or want assistance in specific situations. In addition to the Gemini app, Guided Vision is also available in Google TalkBack, or users can set up an accessibility shortcut for it in the Settings app on devices running Android 9 and above, after it was announced in a recent set of Pixel updates .
You can also ask follow-up questions about whatever you’re looking at, like asking Gemini to read off the expiration date on an item it helped you find. Google says Gemini will give you audio cues to help line up your camera if you ask about something that’s not in the shot. However, Google cautions users not to rely on Guided Vision for things like “navigation, safe-travel guidance, or obstacle detection,” or as a replacement for a cane or mobility aid.

articles.title_orig: Of Note: A Future Marine Corps Commandant’s World War I Anniversary Letter
articles.title_zh: Of Note: A Future Marine Corps Commandant’s World War I Anniversary Letter
articles.content_orig:
A 2022 addition to the John Archer Lejeune Papers in the Library of Congress Manuscript Division consists entirely of his letters home to his wife Ellie Murdaugh Lejeune during World War I. At the time, the future Commandant of the United States Marine Corps was a major general commanding the Army’s 2 nd Division as part of the American Expeditionary Forces. While many of his letters home describe wartime events, they also show a softer side not often associated with a man commonly referred to as “the greatest Leatherneck of them all.”
Perhaps the most tender of these is an October 23, 1918, letter in which John celebrated their anniversary alone while reflecting on his happy home life. “This is the anniversary of our wedding day, 23 years have passed by since that wonderful day and each year has been happier than its predecessor.” The separation gnawed at him. He wrote to Ellie, “I wish with all my heart that I were home with you tonight, so we could look at the moon and the stars together and tell each other of our love.” The photos of his wife and daughters that John lined up on his mantle were a poor substitute for the real thing.
Despite his responsibilities, the day found John in a wistful, nostalgic mood. “I have thought of you darling all the day long and have pictured to myself over and over again just how beautiful you were in your wedding dress. I can never forget those fleeting moments during the ceremony when we took our vows to each other and to God.” When the Lejeunes married in a small ceremony in the parlor of Ellie’s family home in 1895, she had worn a white crepe dress for the occasion.
Even a wedding anniversary could not keep the war away, however. Interspersed with the sentimentality was an update on the war. “My most earnest prayer is that peace may soon return to the world and that we may then be reunited never more to part,” wrote John. “Victory must be near though the road to be trod is still a bloody one.” As he did in many of his letters, John kept Ellie updated on his duties as a military officer. Ellie, in turn, served as John’s sounding board while he was away, along with keeping the household running.
John and Ellie were finally reunited the next summer in 1919 upon the war’s end. As John hurried down the gangplank of the USS George Washington , Ellie and their three daughters met him on the dock at Hoboken, New Jersey, to welcome him home. John and Ellie Lejeune are buried together at Arlington National Cemetery, never more to be parted.

articles.content_orig:

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC , while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
Read More: Trump’s Title IX Announcement Is Cruel. But It Does Not Change the Law
Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
Cornell responded in a statement last week, saying that it could not confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes due to student privacy laws. However, the university clarified on Monday that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
“We take sexual violence extremely seriously,” the Sept. 21 statement said. “The Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched shortly after this incident and issued a REPORT in March 2026.”
In a statement Monday, Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter closed in 2024 and the fraternity remains barred from campus.
But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.
Patel points to Doe’s attorney’s account of her efforts to leave Cornell after the alleged assault. In a Sept. 28 interview with CNN, Thomas Giuffra—Jane Doe’s lawyer—said Cornell refused her family’s tuition-refund request, leaving her to spend another semester on campus.
“She was trying to leave the institution; she didn’t want to be there,” Patel says.
Cornell told People that it works with students seeking to take leave or withdraw and “regularly refunds payments if students are no longer enrolled.”
Giuffra also told CNN that Doe is no longer in college as of 2026.
Universities also have obligations to offer support regardless of a formal complaint or a finding of culpability. These can include counseling, academic adjustments, and housing or schedule changes. Patel says it remains unclear whether Cornell fully complied with its Title IX obligations because the supportive measures it provided Doe are not publicly known.
Regardless, the situation raises questions about what more schools can do for students, Patel says, providing some examples of the types of questions that a university might ask in the aftermath of this kind of incident: “Does she need extensions on exams? Does she need some time off, some leave? Does she need a housing shift if the fraternity house and her sorority house are close together? Does she need counseling? Did they provide a stay away order? What kind of support were they giving her to make sure she wouldn’t have to be retriggered and traumatized by running into them?”
Title IX also requires schools to investigate allegations through a reliable, impartial process—independently of criminal court systems, and using a lower burden of proof to determine if a student violated campus policy.
Cornell University publicly disclosed that it was investigating the allegation on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe went to the police, according to the lawsuit. The university sent an alert to students regarding a report of sexual assault and coercion into taking drugs at a fraternity house. The same day, Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity.
In response to an inquiry from TIME, Cornell said that its “Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated the allegations against the individuals and the fraternity consistent with university policies and Title IX.”
“The university’s Title IX investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days,” the university’s statement continued. “The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence in the university’s investigation.”
Cornell’s handling of the case unfolded amid shifting federal rules on campus sexual misconduct. A court vacated the Biden Administration’s Title IX rule on Jan. 9, 2025—five days before Cornell began its formal investigation, according to Doe’s complaint. The university held hearings that May, making the rules it applied a key question in assessing its response.
The Biden Administration had expanded Title IX regulations in April 2024—taking effect in August 2024—broadening the definition of sexual harassment and extending federal protections.
On Jan. 9, 2025, however, a federal district court issued a decision vacating the 2024 Biden rule nationwide. This week, the Trump Administration formally restored the 2020 Title IX regulations to the Code of Federal Regulations. Those rules, introduced during Pres

articles.title_orig: Tyler Erb Reflects on ‘Exponential’ Growth in First Year Back With World of Outlaws
articles.title_zh: Tyler Erb Reflects on ‘Exponential’ Growth in First Year Back With World of Outlaws
articles.content_orig:
October 1, 2026 at 3:27 pm
For the first time in a long time, Tyler Erb is approaching the end of a full-time national tour run in a positive frame of mind.
The New Waverly, TX native spent three years with the World of Outlaws Late Model Series presented by DIRTVision from 2016 through 2018, before shifting to the Lucas Oil Late Model Dirt Series from 2019 until 2023. Erb amassed 21 wins between them and a best points finish of fourth in 2019, but three years ago, he knew it was time for a change.
The next two seasons in 2024 and 2025 were what Erb affectionately called the “Fun Tour” – racing wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted. His travels produced 33 wins over two years, plus the 2024 DIRTcar Summer Nationals championship.
“Last time I ran a national tour, I was just mad at the world,” Erb said. “I had done it for, I don’t know, six, seven years actually. I was burned out because I didn’t feel like I got to go to some of the places I wanted to go. I didn’t get to race a whole year the way I thought I wanted to race, and that’s just do whatever I want to do, pick and choose. Not skip races, but just go to the ones that I feel like I had a really good chance to win. I got to do that for two years and was successful doing it.
“So, then I was like, ‘OK, I feel like I’ve done really good at picking and choosing and doing all that.’ So, I can check that off my list of stuff, self-goals that I have that no one cares about except me. And the next one I have would be to try to win an Outlaws championship. And in order to do that, you’ve got to do it and compete.”
That’s precisely what Erb and his Best Performance Motorsports team set out to do in their return to full-time World of Outlaws racing in 2026. Erb’s refreshed mindset and renewed sense of confidence has resulted in what could be described as the best year of his career. With five races remaining in the season, Erb sits in a career-high third in the championship standings, trailing only the two hottest Late Model drivers in America in Bobby Pierce and Nick Hoffman .
“I had kind of set my own goals, and being third in points is kind of within that range,” Erb said. “Winning four races is a little light on, you know, how many I was trying to win this year. But we still have five left or whatever, so there’s definitely a chance to make up for a lot of it. I would give it a B+, A-. Because Nick and Bobby are obviously really, really good. To be right there behind them and beat them on the nights we beat them, I feel like that’s good.”
It’s often said that you’re only as good as the competition you race against, and Erb credits his own progression this year to battling the same elite cast of characters night after night. It has made his own spot in the pecking order plain to see, as well as the areas that need to improve to take the next step into championship contention next season.
“Like right now, Nick and Bobby are ranked first and second in the [DirtonDirt] poll,” Erb said. “If you beat them however many times, you’re like, ‘OK, well, I beat them last week, so I can beat them this week.’ Where if you come in and you don’t beat them, and then you watch for a month and they run second, second, second and you win, you’re like, ‘Oh, I’ll beat them guys no problem.’ When you race them every night, you kind of realize their strengths and weaknesses and get an idea of how to beat them. It’s been good. You race some of the best competition night in, night out, it just makes you better.
“Going racing at different places and the stuff I did before definitely helps too, because you just race at all sorts of different racetracks and series and rules, you have to be able to adapt quick. But doing what we’re doing now, I think in the long run, the growth I’ve had this year is probably exponential compared to what I did the two years before. But I needed the two years of racing the ‘Fun Tour’ per se to grow in that aspect.”
Erb has never been afraid of doing things his own way both on and off the track. His car choice is one example, as Erb is one of only two World of Outlaws full-timers flying the flag for Rocket Chassis. That has created a bond between Erb and 2022 World of Outlaws champion Dennis Erb Jr. that goes back several years, and being in the same pit area every night has only strengthened the relationship.
“Dennis is an older me,” Erb said. “He’s done it, he’s kind of hard-headed, kind of his own person and there’s nothing wrong with that. I mean, for both of our sakes, if we won every race and it was the Dennis and Tyler show, that would be cool. It’s good to have somebody that you can lean on at times, and I feel like I do that for Dennis and Dennis does that for me with anything. His approach to a race and my approach, everybody’s a little bit different in a sense, but it is nice that I’m not the only lone ranger out there.
“I have Dennis, and then when Mark [Richards] or Josh Rice or whoever shows up, we all want to do good. We’re outnumbered to an extent right now, but I don’t look at it that way; I could care less. I know what I’m comfortable in and what I drive, and I think everybody in a Rocket has that same mindset. We’ve been in them for so long, it’s just what we’re comfortable with. We can make it work because we win races; we’ve just got to do it on a more consistent level.”
As Erb prepares to close the book on 2026 and look ahead to next season, he’s doing so at a point in life many dream of. His race team is on the rise and running up front more than ever, and away from the track, he’s about to become a first-time father with fiancée Emma Hodge. But is the rambunctious, short-fused Erb of old finally growing up? He’s not so sure.
“Nobody grows up, that’s such bulls**t,” Erb said. “I just know what I want to do, I’m very focused on it and have figured out how to balance it a little bit. Obviously, I’m getting married, having a kid, so that’s super exciting. I didn’t have any of that three years ago. I didn’t even know if I wanted that; I didn’t have an idea about it. Now, I’m very sure of what I want to do and get done, so it’s just a different mindset. Time goes on and opens your eyes to a lot of things.”
Erb will wrap up his season with the World of Outlaws Late Model Series presented by DIRTVision in the Modoc 100 at Modoc Speedway (Friday-Saturday, Oct. 23-24), followed by the Dave Smith Motors World of Outlaws World Finals at The Dirt Track at Charlotte (Wednesday-Saturday, Nov. 4-7). articles.title_orig: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.title_zh: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.content_orig:
We don’t yet know how the 2026 midterm elections will shake out.
What we can say right now is that President Donald Trump’s handling of inflation is a historic liability — the likes of which we’ve rarely seen in modern American politics.
As many as 8 in 10 Americans now disapprove of Trump on that issue. That’s more than disapproved of presidents for wars gone wrong, botched crisis responses and even major scandals like Watergate.
A new AP-NORC poll on Thursday was the latest ugly data point for Trump. It showed Americans disapproved of him on cost-of-living issues by a stunning margin: 82% to 17%.
It’s rare to get even 70% of Americans to agree on anything political. But Trump has managed to unite 8 in 10 Americans against his handling of one of the country’s most important issues.
And this poll isn’t just some outlier. Here’s a brief recap of recent polls on this issue:
The level of disapproval on such a major issue has few precedents, though George W. Bush did face a 77% disapproval rating in a CBS News/New York Times poll for his handling of the economy near the end of his term after the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980, the same pollster showed Jimmy Carter’s disapproval on that issue peaking at 74% amid high unemployment and inflation.
One of the likeliest culprits for such high disapproval numbers would seem to be war. And those have been very unpopular. But not as unpopular as Trump’s handling of the cost of living. George W. Bush’s disapproval rating on the Iraq war peaked around 70% . Disapproval of Joe Biden’s withdrawal from Afghanistan peaked around two-thirds . And the Vietnam war led Lyndon Johnson to scrap his reelection bid in 1968, but his disapproval rating on the issue was only in the 60s .
In fact, the highest disapproval rating for a war appears to be Trump’s latest numbers on the Iran war. The CNN poll showed 73% disapproved of his handling of that.
When it comes to crises, as many as 64% disapproved of Bush’s handling of Hurricane Katrina, and Carter’s disapproval amid the Iran hostage crisis climbed into the mid-50s. Even Trump’s handling of the January 6 attack on the Capitol ( 67% in CNN polling ) wasn’t as lopsided as Trump and inflation right now.
As far as scandals, Ronald Reagan’s disapproval on the Iran-Contra affair reached as high as 69% in a January 1987 Washington Post-ABC News poll. And at the height of Watergate, as many as 71% of Americans disapproved of Richard Nixon on domestic issues. (We don’t have good approval polling from back then on Watergate, specifically.)
Speaking of Nixon, pardons have also tested Americans’ tolerance. But even Gerald Ford’s pardon of Nixon — which was supposed to have crippled Ford politically — only saw a disapproval rating in the 50s , according to polls compiled by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research.
Indeed, about the closest Trump got previously to 80% disapproval on a major issue was another controversial set of pardons: his pardons of violent January 6 defendants last year. A Pew Research Center poll showed 74% of Americans disapproved of that.
You might be noticing a trend here. Many of the issues with the highest presidential disapproval ratings involve the same president: Trump. That includes the Iran war, the January 6 Capitol attack and the related pardons. But the disapproval he faces on inflation surpasses all of those issues.
You could perhaps understand why Republicans are suddenly anxious to pass legislation on affordability before the election.
Trump in a new Time magazine interview published Thursday said Americans shouldn’t hold him responsible for their affordability problems and again blamed inflation on Biden. (This despite inflation being higher today than it was when Trump took over last year.)
But the AP-NORC poll is the latest to suggest that strategy won’t work. It shows 65% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for high prices more so than factors beyond his control. That number for Biden just before the 2022 midterm elections was much lower: 44% .
Perhaps Trump’s party can still do OK in the upcoming midterms. But if it does, it will be despite historic dissatisfaction with the president on voters’ clear No. 1 issue.

articles.title_orig: World ski body eyes financial reset after overspending and wants to add new events - ABC News
articles.title_zh: World ski body eyes financial reset after overspending and wants to add new events - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Skiing’s governing body was on track to spend all its cash reserves by 2028 and has now cut jobs while aiming to add new competitions to restore finances
GENEVA -- Skiing’s governing body was on track to spend all its cash reserves by 2028 and has now cut jobs while aiming to add new events to help restore finances.
The International Ski and Snowboard Federation’s rescue plan — steering away from expected annual losses of 20 million Swiss francs ($24 million) — was detailed at meetings this week ahead of the first winter season since new president Alexander Ospelt from Liechtenstein was elected by a single vote.
Rising concerns about spending during the five-year presidency of Johan Eliasch , the billionaire boss of the Head ski and sportswear brand, seemed to be decisive in the June election.
“We are in a serious situation, not a desperate one,” the ski body’s interim secretary general Urs Lehmann said in an interview on the sidelines of the week-long gathering in Geneva. “The FIS family deserved to have clarity where we are.”
An FIS office in Munich, Germany was closed and race prize money subsidies that began during the COVID-19 pandemic have been curbed. It's part of the financial reset for the governing body that oversees Alpine and cross-country skiing, freestyle and snowboarding, ski jumping and Nordic combined.
The World Cup race earnings leaders across the FIS disciplines last winter were the superstars of Alpine skiing who also won their overall titles.
Switzerland's Marco Odermatt won 741,000 euros ($832,000) in prize money from race organizers and Mikaela Shiffrin topped the women's list with 615,000 euros ($690,000) earned. Yet they were the only Alpine skiers to earn more than 400,000 euros ($450,000) from races across the five-month season.
Those totals also were boosted by FIS money that started during the pandemic and is no longer viable.
“If you add something, that’s easy," Lehmann, the 1993 men’s downhill world champion for Switzerland, told The Associated Press. “Taking it away again is super difficult and nobody did it over the last three years.”
Maintaining and increasing athlete prize money likely will mean more races spread around more venues that want to either join or be a more regular stop on the World Cup circuits.
“There is only one way — add competitions," Lehmann said. “Can we do this? Yes, because I’m a strong believer that our calendar has more space. We have more interested parties than we have spots today.”
Extra world championships are set to be added in the current down year of a four-year Olympic cycle which includes two editions of worlds.
Member federations were told at a specially convened FIS Summit in Geneva that “FIS is solvent today but in a critical point," according to a presentation.
Equity reserves had almost halved at the end of last year to about 43 million Swiss francs ($52 million) since 2021 when Eliasch was elected, after a second pandemic-hit season.
Total revenue for the four-year cycle through 2029 is set to double to almost 650 million Swiss francs ($783 million) yet expenses are rising at a faster rate.
Reserves are set to be exhausted by the end of the 2028 winter season, with reasons cited including a decline in the value of world championships broadcasting rights and rising broadcast production costs.
FIS members were told their governing body had been paying them too much while its staffing almost doubled from 50 to 98.
“We had to let go a bunch of our teammates unfortunately to become leaner, more efficient and also cost efficient,” said Lehmann, who joined FIS in a newly created chief executive role last year then resigned days before the presidential election.
“We have a plan but this plan works only if the FIS family is really standing together,” Lehmann said.
Long-term broadcast and commercial contracts mean the situation cannot change fast enough.
“In media rights, basically the deals are done until 2030. The effect of having a higher value we will only see in almost four years,” Lehmann said. "I am convinced that we are going to make it but everybody has to know where we stand today.”

articles.title_orig: School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France
articles.title_zh: School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France
articles.content_orig:
French students have set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.
Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.
Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.
At Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school, the teachers were inadvertently splashed as a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. Earlier, the prosecutor’s office had ⁠said the teachers had been assaulted and “doused in petrol”.
At another school in the city, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a firetruck that had arrived to put out a blaze in the morning, police said. The attackers forced the firefighters to flee the vehicle, then set it alight.
In Nantes, firefighters extinguished a fire at a high school entrance following what regional education officials called a gathering “marked by violence towards staff”. In Strasbourg, trams were halted to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, and students burned barriers on tram tracks, authorities said.
“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius [95 degrees Fahrenheit] in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael, a 17-year-old who withheld his surname for fear of reprisals, told the AFP news agency outside a protest in Strasbourg.
“The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors.”
His frustration echoes a wave of student anger that has spread across France since last week, as high school pupils protest and grievances snowball into nationwide unrest.
Some 340 demonstrations were under way outside high schools by mid-morning on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down as a result, police said.
University students joined in, blocking access to about 30 campuses, including in Paris and Marseille, according to a student union.
Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries – some from thrown objects, others reportedly from police riot-control projectiles.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police have opened internal investigations into brutality allegations involving three students.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting and asked ministers to cancel upcoming official travel so authorities could focus on the demonstrations, his office said.
French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that he would successively meet representative staff unions and parent and student associations on Friday.
The unrest has become entangled in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron next May. The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed party of encouraging the protests. Presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Wednesday that his party “called for nonviolent methods of struggle” and criticised the government’s response as repressive.

articles.title_orig: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.title_zh: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.content_orig:
While one million children around the world offered up the Rosary for peace, about 1,300 of those voices were coming from the Vatican Gardens on the first day of the month dedicated to the RosaryâOctober 1. Children from parishes and schools around Rome gathered at the Grotto of Lourdes with Pope Leo XIV to kick off the Aid to the Church in Need initiative âOne Million Children Praying the Rosaryâ.
Representing the global dimension of this initiative, each of the five decades was recited in a different language: Italian, Spanish, Urdu, German, and Arabic.
This rosary starts a weeklong initiative drawing attention to âthe wounds and hopes of peoplesâ globallyâthe children of Ukraine and all the victims of war; families in Lebanon, Syria, and the Holy Land; persecuted Christians in Pakistan and around the world; reconciliation in South Sudan; and families in Cuba and Venezuela.
Before reciting the Marian prayer, Cardinal Kurt Koch, Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, explained that this initiative is an invitation for children to discover that âtogether with Mary, they can bring the sufferings of the world to Jesus.â
âIt is precisely the voices of the youngest, who entrust themselves to him with confidence, that find a special welcome in the heart of God,â he stressed. Throughout the weekâOctober 1-7âcommunities around the world, separated by language and distance, will be united in their prayer for peace.
âAs we contemplate the risen Christ, we ask that fear and hatred may not have the final word,â Cardinal Koch said.
In his message, Pope Leo XIV stressed the importance of this initiative and his joy at being present with the children, parents, and priests.
Encouraging the children, the Pope reminded them that they are asking Jesus and Mary for âa special gift: peace for all the children of the world, especially those who live in places where there is war, in so many countries around the world.â
He described the rosary as a âsimple prayer that everyone can prayâ and called the flowers the children had offered at the beginning of each decade as a sign of love.
The Pope urged them to think about Jesus at the important moments of his life, âwhen he brought light and peace to many people.â These included Jesusâ baptism in the Jordan, turning water in wine at the wedding of Cana, proclaiming the Kingdom of God, his Transfiguration, and when he instituted the Eucharist in the Upper Room.
Pope Leo urged the children never to forget and be thankful for these moments when Jesus âgave us wonderful giftsâ and to âask him with confidence, all united: Give us peaceâ.
Concluding his message to the children and families, the Pope highlighted how those present in the Vatican Gardens throughout this week (October 1-7) are not the only ones praying. About one million voices are joining them in this prayer.
âThink about itâ, Pope Leo stressed: âFifty million âHail Marysâ rising to Heaven from every part of the world and in every language, asking for peace, joining together like one enormous Rosary, embracing all the continents, peoples, and nations of the world.â
By praying the rosary together at the Grotto of Lourdes, he reminded everyone present that they are committing themselves to behaving well wherever they are: at home, school, in catechism class, with their parents, and when they play.
âPrayers must also be accompanied by good deeds and acts of love,â Pope Leo explained. âThat is how peace grows.â

articles.title_orig: Sony announces QSSR AI upscaling tech for base PS5 in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei
articles.title_zh: Sony announces QSSR AI upscaling tech for base PS5 in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei
articles.content_orig:
Sony has announced QSSR - Quick Spectral Super Resolution - bringing PSSR-style AI upscaling to the base PS5 in a huge coup for existing console owners. Games need to be updated to add support for QSSR, but two are already ready: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
It was thought to be impossible for PSSR to work on the base PS5, as it lacks the dedicated AI upscaling hardware necessary, but Sony has managed to bring a version of the technology to PS5 that is performant enough to be worth using - hence the "quick" part of the name.
We've already tested QSSR and early impressions are excellent - but how does this work, anyway?
In short, the firms used a more streamlined neural network architecture to fit into the PS5's limited hardware acceleration, and a hand-tuned implementation that trades off accuracy for performance. PSSR ought to always produce better-looking results, thanks to running on 300 TOPS of dedicated hardware in PS5 Pro, but QSSR should in turn outperform existing software-based upscaling and anti-aliasing solutions on the base PS5, like industry-standard TAA, Epic's Unreal Engine TSR and AMD's FSR 3 - especially when it comes to image stability.
Here's head of technology Mike Fitzgerald at Insomniac Games, developers of Marvel's Wolverine:
"QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan's epic journey. It's a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel's Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5."
And here's lead rendering engineer Jasmin Patry at Sucker Punch Productions, the studio behind Ghost of Yōtei:
"At Sucker Punch, we’re excited to bring QSSR to Ghost of Yōtei players so that they can experience the world we’ve created with even more clarity and detail. QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn’t been possible on the PS5 console until now. We’ve long wished that all PS5 players could experience the incredible image quality that PSSR brings to PS5 Pro, and QSSR is a positive step towards that goal!"
QSSR will be freely available for other PlayStation developers to implement now that it's officially been unveiled, and ought to be widely adopted. Any game with PSSR support can add QSSR support very easily, almost as a drop-in replacement that only requires some settings tweaks to suit the new level of performance.
Games that don't support PSSR can also be retrofitted with slightly more development work, and of course studios with upcoming PlayStation releases can also take QSSR into account much earlier in the development process to make full use of the tech. For example, I suspect the authors of Grand Theft Auto 6 could have just enough time to integrate QSSR if they so choose.
We have much more detail in our QSSR feature , based on several conversations with Sony engineers, so I'd encourage you to read that next if you haven't already.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.title_zh: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.content_orig:
Annual update installed. You're up to date, so nothing seems to have changed. Wait a minute...
Windows 11 26H2 is out, and Microsoft has enabled Windows settings backup by default, a move that could send administrators scrambling to opt out where they once had to opt in.
The latest release hasn't made a lot of shockwaves in the community featurewise. Users with up-to-date versions of 25H2 will unlikely notice much difference – 26H2 has the same code base, delivered via an enablement package. It even has the same set of known issues, although all are now "mitigated" in one way or another.
However, administrators will spot several important changes. The end-of-support clock is reset, and Microsoft has flipped some switches behind the scenes; notably, enabling Windows backup and restore (formerly Windows Backup for Organizations) by default.
The service, which was previously off by default, backs up a device's settings and a list of installed Microsoft Store apps. The idea is that when a user moves to a new device, a restore can happen during setup. Microsoft also listed an objective of the service as allowing "organizations to transition to a cloud-first approach for managing devices and user settings."
The problem is that many organizations are prohibited from sending this data to the cloud. As a result, the default-on setting won't apply in privacy-sensitive regions such as those covered by the EU Digital Markets Act, or in sovereign and restricted environments.
For many others running Windows 11 26H2, it'll now be enabled by default on eligible devices – Entra joined or Entra Hybrid joined. Unless an administrator has explicitly said no to the functionality, the act of installing the update will flip the switch, and the backups will begin.
Administrators will rightly be wary of anything that switches from opt-in to opt-out, even something so apparently useful and innocuous as a backup. Why wouldn't you want your users to be able to leap to a new device with ease? That assumes their data is also in the cloud, of course, since this only backs up settings and a list of Windows apps. Backing up data is something else entirely.
That is the real issue with the change. The release of Windows 11 26H2 isn't particularly exciting in itself, but flipping a long-standing opt-in to opt-out as part of it is likely to set more than a few nerves jangling. ®

articles.title_orig: ‘From conflict to communion’: Lutheran World Federation meets with Pope
articles.title_zh: ‘From conflict to communion’: Lutheran World Federation meets with Pope
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo met on Thursday morning with a delegation from the Lutheran World Federation, expressing his appreciation for the way Catholic-Lutheran relations have âmatured both spiritually and theologically over the decadesâ. Among those in attendance was the Rev Dr Anne Burghardt, the Federationâs General Secretary and an ordained pastor in the Estonian Evangelical Lutheran Church.
After the meeting, she stopped by for an interview in Vatican Newsâ offices, discussing Catholic-Lutheran relations, synodality, and the upcoming 500 th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession, a foundational Lutheran text.
The following transcript has been lightly edited for style and brevity
Q: How did your meeting with the Pope go?
A: It was a very cordial atmosphere. Itâs always a pleasure to come to visit the Vatican. Sometimes we tend to forget how much ecumenical movement has achieved, but nowadays it really feels like coming to visit sisters and brothers in Christ.
Weâre now moving towards celebrating 500 years of Augsburg Confession, which the Pope mentioned in his speech, expressing his hope for the ecumenical potential of this process. For me personally, it was the second time meeting Pope Leo, because I was able to come to his inauguration. But for most of our delegation it was the first time meeting him, and we perceived him as very attentive, very present, very thoughtful and very open.
In his speech to you, Pope Leo mentioned the ongoing Lutheran-Catholic dialogue process. What can you tell me about that?
We have had a bilateral dialogue with Catholic Church since 1967. It started right after the Second Vatican Council. And in the current phase, we are looking into ways to come up with a joint understanding or joint statement on the Augsburg Confession, which is a confession that has real relevance for Lutheran churches across the world.
Although it is often seen as a confessional document, its content has a highly ecumenical potential in terms of bringing different Churches together around some of the main questions of our faith: How do we understand God? How do we how do we understand Jesus Christ? How do we understand justification, and how we understand the Church?
One of the big concerns of the Catholic Church at the moment is the ongoing synodal process. I know you've spoken before about its ecumenical significance ...
We were very grateful that that Catholic Church also invited ecumenical guests to participate in the synod. Our assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations attended the second synod session and came back with very positive impressions about how inclusively the whole process had been set up, how lay people had also been given voice.
In a way, the fact of lay participation is not new for Lutherans. This has been our practise for centuries - to include lay voices in in church governing bodies. But it is very good to see this opening also in the Catholic Church. We, on the other hand, probably need to move in the other direction, to make sure that that our member churches are more aware of being members of one communion, where they are of course all autonomous, but at the same time in, as we call it, âaltar and pulpitâ fellowship with one another. In that sense, it is very interesting to see these two processes unfolding side by side.
You gave the Pope two gifts. What were they and why?
One of them was the so-called Lund Cross. Back in 2016, we commemorated the 500 year anniversary of the Reformation together with the Catholic Church and with Pope Francis. The joint commemoration took place in October in 2016 in Lund, in Sweden, in the cathedral. The special Lund cross was designed for that event, and we gave a replica to Pope Leo today in hope that we will continue on this journey from conflict to communion.
The other gift was a ceramic bowl, with the symbol of a pomegranate and also a dove as a symbol of peace. It was made by the students of vocational training centre in East Jerusalem, where our Augusta Victoria Hospital serves Palestinian patients and offers cancer care, which almost none of the other hospitals do for Palestinians in this region.

articles.title_orig: Renee Good family lawyers invoke anti-KKK law in suing U.S., federal agents
articles.title_zh: Renee Good family lawyers invoke anti-KKK law in suing U.S., federal agents
articles.content_orig:
Create an account or log in to save stories.
Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories.
Lawyers for the family of Renee Good on Thursday invoked an 1871 law meant to fight the terror of the Ku Klux Klan as they filed two civil lawsuits seeking accountability for Good’s killing by a federal agent during Operation Metro Surge.
The lawsuits name Jonathan Ross — the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot Good — as well as current and former Trump administration officials, including Gregory Bovino, Kristi Noem, Tom Homan and Stephen Miller.
“The day of accountability has arrived for our own U.S. government and its governmental agencies,” attorney Antonio Romanucci told reporters Thursday as he stood beside Good’s family after filing the lawsuits. “Our government is killing our citizens without any legal justification.”
The lawsuits seek accountability for the decisions of public officials and federal agents as well as damages “for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses” suffered by her family.
MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all.
“She was the love of my life,” Becca Good, Renee’s partner, told reporters Thursday in her first public remarks since witnessing Renee’s killing. “She was funny and she was smart and she was gorgeous. She was the center of my universe. You don’t know how much light someone gives you until it’s gone.”
She spoke through tears of Good’s three children. “No child should grow up without a parent. No one should lose their sister or their daughter. No one should have to live without their soulmate,” she added. “True accountability and change is the only way to make sure no family has to go through what we have."
Renee Good was shot and killed inside her vehicle by Ross, the ICE agent, on the morning of Jan. 7 in south Minneapolis, near East 34th Street and Portland Avenue. She and her wife had stopped to observe ICE agents gathering at the location.
Federal authorities quickly called the shooting justified , saying 37-year-old Good tried to run down ICE agents with her vehicle and that the agent — later identified as Ross — fired to protect his life and the lives of other officers.
Bystander video, however, contradicted that narrative. Eyewitnesses said agents gave Good conflicting orders about whether to stay or go, and that she appeared to just want to leave the scene.
Ross, the ICE agent who fatally shot Good, was one of thousands of federal immigration agents that flooded the Twin Cites over the winter in Operation Metro Surge. Federal officials said they were searching to find and deport the “worst of the worst,” but that’s not what happened.
Data later showed that fewer than 25 percent of those arrested had a criminal conviction on their record. A little more than 13 percent of those arrested had pending criminal charges.
The White House used “unfounded and exaggerated accusations” about fraud in Minnesota to send masked agents into Minneapolis neighborhoods to “harass people based on how they looked” and led those agents to believe they wouldn’t face consequences for their actions, said attorney Benjamin Berkman.
The second of the two civil suits invokes the Ku Klux Klan act of 1871 .
Congress passed that law at the time “because masked men were going in disguise on the highway to terrorize their neighbors on account of their race,” Berkman said. One hundred fifty-five years later, armed men went in disguise on Portland Avenue. They went as part of campaign to terrorize people based on the way they looked — and now Renee Good is dead.”
Using the anti-Ku Klux Klan law, he added, “reaches the agent who fired those shots and every public official who put him on the street that day.”
The Department of Justice, responding to an inquiry from MPR News, said it “declines to comment on pending litigation or investigations.”
A message left with the Department of Homeland Security, seeking response to the lawsuits, was not immediately returned.
A post shared by MPR News (@mprnews)
Vigils for Renee Good popped up across Minnesota hours after she was killed, as the state found itself at the center of a national debate on immigration enforcement.
Two and a half weeks later, federal agents in Minneapolis shot and killed 37-year-old Alex Pretti on Jan. 24 near 26th Street and Nicollet Avenue.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Pretti was armed with a handgun, that a struggle ensued as agents tried to subdue him and that an agent “fired defensive shots.” But video and eyewitness testimony again disputed federal officials’ account.
MPR News reporter Jon Collins contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Latest taxpayer-funded ad promotes Trump war with Iran
articles.title_zh: Latest taxpayer-funded ad promotes Trump war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
A GOP senator blocked a resolution on Tuesday that criticized the Trump administration’s recent taxpayer-funded ads promoting President Donald Trump.
Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming objected to the Democrat-led measure, which stated that taxpayer funds should not have been used for the controversial ads.
The measure, from Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, slammed the administration for using government funds for the White House’s recent advertisements. “It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language ‘paid for by the U.S. Government,’ should not be paid for by the United States government,” it read.
Senators on both sides of the aisle have criticized the president for using taxpayer dollars for the ads. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday, “It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” and retiring GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas added, “no” it’s not appropriate. “It’s not even a close question,” he said.
On the Senate floor on Tuesday, as she introduced her resolution, Hassan said, “The American people want their tax dollars to go towards helping them and keeping them safe, not propaganda campaigns for a president. He’s welcome to run whatever ads he wants with his own riches, but with taxpayer dollars, money that people have worked hard to earn, he needs to follow the law.”
Lummis echoed the White House’s own argument that the ads are comparable to public service announcements released during previous administrations, and are not campaign ads.
“Presidents of both parties have used public service announcements to speak directly to the American people for decades,” the Wyoming Republican said. “The message at the heart of these PSAs is a simple one: American values are worth defending against the failed ideologies of communism and socialism. If that is what has the senator from New Hampshire concerned, I’d suggest the concern says more about her side of the aisle than it does about the PSA.”
One recently released taxpayer-funded television ad features imagery of Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad .
Hassan attempted to pass the resolution criticizing the use of taxpayer funding for the ads via a fast-track process known as a unanimous consent request. Any single senator can object to such a request.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday defended the ads, arguing they are not political because he is not on the ballot.
“Well, I’m not running for office, first of all, and so the ads are given by me, but I’m not running for office, and I don’t talk about anybody,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
The president described the spots as patriotic messaging rather than campaign material. “But when I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo: World needs ecumenical witnesses to Christ
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo: World needs ecumenical witnesses to Christ
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV held an audience on Thursday with respresentatives of the Lutheran World Federation.
In his address, the Pope expressed his appreciation that Lutheran-Catholic relations have matured spiritually and theologically over the past few decades.
He pointed to the ongoing international dialogue between the Lutheran and Catholic Churches, which has reached its sixth phase.
Pope Leo then recalled the late Pope Francisâ invitation in 2021 to ecumenism, which he said purifies memories and overcomes inflexible attitudes.
âEcumenism is not an exercise of ecclesial diplomacy but a journey of grace,â he said. âIt depends not on human negotiations and agreements, but on the grace of Godâ.
Pope Leo encouraged Catholics and Lutherans to continue on that journey.
âRenewed communion in the apostolic faith, in the sacraments, and in the ministries is the goal of our ecumenical journey of grace, which we walk together guided by the Gospel,â he said.
The Pope noted that 2030 will mark the 500th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession, saying that what became a divisive moment should now instead be an opportunity for a âprofound ecumenical experienceâ that takes Christians closer to full, visible unity.
He recalled Pope St. John Paul IIâs words about the Augsburg Confession, saying the authorsâ intention was to bear witness to âtheir faith in the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church.â
Meant as a document of reconciliation within the Church, the Confessio Augustana later came to be understood as a âtext of divisive confessionalization.â
Pope Leo invited all Christians, especially theologians, to set their minds and hearts on Christ, as the Churches look toward the 2030 anniversary.
âLet us return, with deep devotion,â he said, âto our common roots, to the faith of the early Church and the Church Fathers, in order to rediscover the apostolic and pre-confessional heritage which truly unites us as brothers and sisters in Christ.â
In conclusion, Pope Leo XIV said Christ must not become a âforeign wordâ in our world, inviting Lutherans and Catholics to share our common missionary task of preaching the Gospel.
âOur world needs ecumenical witnesses to Christ who make him known through their lives and actions,â he said, âfor He alone is the living source capable of fulfilling humanityâs deepest longings.â

articles.title_orig: Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender
articles.title_zh: Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender
articles.content_orig:
The risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States reveals
A mid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.
The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was the Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public’s, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.
The California governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a mandate to create an “ AI kill-switch ”; New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul , is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ ban artificial superintelligence ”.
While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported.
A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but by government reliance on error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent.
A CNN report published on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three.
It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents.
Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots.
We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare.
Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”.
In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible-looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users.
CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was probably fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise from deliberate mystification on the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it.
Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because people believe that the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are.
From “AI” scribes used by hospitals erroneously classifying patients as illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems which mistake schools for military facilities , we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software.
Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom.
It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions.
As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption from the law when it comes to AI : there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “ magic intelligence in the sky ”.
Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points.
Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist , which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.
Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author of The AI Con .
